speechtext:
The debate on the budget has now been concluded. The house has taken steps by appropriate resolutions to facilitate its consideration of the business of the session still to be dealt with.
I thought, therefore, it would be opportune and meet with the approval of the hon. members if I drew attention to one of the rules of the house that has been frequently disregarded in previous debates, and perhaps particularly in the debate that has just finished.
Suggestions are frequently made with regard to amendments to the rules governing the business of the house, and I have no doubt these could be improved. However, I would point out to hon. members that rules are of little value unless they are observed, and that this can be achieved only by the cooperation of hon. members themselves.
The rule to which I have referred is that a member when speaking should not read from a written, previously prepared speech. As early as the year 1886, the House of Commons of that day .adopted the following resolution:
That the growing practice in the Canadian House of Commons of delivering speeches of great length, having the character of carefully and elaborately prepared written essays, and indulging in voluminous and often irrelevant extracts, is destructive of legitimate and pertinent debate upon public questions, is a waste of valuable time, unreasonably lengthens the sessions of parliament, threatens by increased bulk and cost to lead to the abolition of the official report of the debates, encourages a discursive and diffuse, rather than an incisive and concise style of public speaking, is a marked contrast to the practice in regard to debate that prevails in the British House of Commons, and tends to repel the public from a careful and intelligent consideration of the proceedings of parliament.
Long usage both in Canada and the United Kingdom has sanctioned the rule that a member while speaking must not read from a written, previously prepared speech-Bourinot, page 335. Bcauchesne's third edition, page 102, May, fourteenth edition, page 417. I am sure hon. members will agree that the best tradition of House of Commons debates is served by a member using his own language and delivering his remarks in the form of an unwritten composition. If the rule were otherwise members might read speeches written by other people and the time of the house
National Housing Act

be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who are not the properly elected representatives of the people.
I have noticed that quite understandably non-observance of the rule by one or more hon. members encourages others to do likewise.
I urge therefore that hon. members give practical recognition to this rule, and in future, refrain from reading their speeches. I am sure that this will be in the best interest of the house and the proper conduct of its business.

speechtext: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved the second reading of Bill No. 176. to amend the National Housing Act, 1944.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to make a few remarks on this bill to amend the National Housing Act. As I understand it, the bill is an attempt to bring down the costs and carrying charges of housing in Canada. The minister is of course approaching the problem by attempting to increase the amortization periods and lower interest charges, which is something for which we should give him credit. Certainly it is a step in the right direction and one might say, so far so good. But I wish to say to him, and I hope to say it in such a way that it *will stick, that he will never get anywhere this way, and we shall never have the lower income groups in this country properly housed by picking at the problem as he is doing.
We have seen in recent weeks the failure of the Housing Enterprises scheme. We know that the wartime housing programme, although very valuable as a temporary measure in these difficult times of housing, offers no long-term solution to the problem of low rent housing. The minister himself has said it is a temporary

measure and that he will withdraw from the field. The fact remains with us, as has been oaid so many times from the opposition benches since I have been in the house, that the housing of the low income groups requires houses for rental at $25 a month or less.
We have rightly been concerned in the past two years with the immediate problem of veterans housing, and that need goes on. I am not discussing that subject at this moment. I have discussed it many times before. But the fact that that need is with us is perhaps hiding from our gaze another important fact, that there is a long-term low-rent housing problem and a slum problem in Canada.
I have here a housing survey made by the Vancouver Housing Association in my own city in 1939 and brought up to date in 1946. It is a most excellent examination of housing conditions in Vancouver, prepared by experts who did years of work on it. It not only sets out arguments for slum clearance and low rent housing but does something else that is very valuable indeed. It gives some facts and figures on the bad housing conditions in a Canadian city. Too often we have to go to United States cities to get these figures.
I wish to give a few excerpts from this report, which will not be all inclusive but yet will give us some idea of housing in one Canadian city today. I will not refer to the particular areas I am talking about. Although they are set out in the report, I do not want to single out any area in Vancouver for unfavourable mention.
The first extract. I want to read is this:
No less than 59 per cent of the houses surveyed in this area were found to he in multiple occupancy, and over 40 per cent of the "rooming" population was living at a density of two or more persons per room. Compare this figure with the commonly accepted minimum standard of room occupation of one person per room . . . The majority of the rooms are rented as housekeeping units, but few of them have adequate facilities for washing, cooking or food storage. Under 10 per cent of the rented rooms had sinks or washbasins and only 5 per cent of the houses in multiple occupancy had more than one bath. Cases of twenty, forty or even fifty persons sharing one bathroom were found. East of Granville street over half the houses were heated by stoves only and a large proportion of the rooms in these houses were inadequately heated.
Referring to another area I read this:
Fifteen per cent of the houses surveyed in this district required major structural repairs; probably at least half of these houses are beyond repair and should be demolished. .Seventeen per cent of the houses lacked baths. Four per cent had outside toilets. Only twenty-five per cent had central heating.
Then referring to another area:
The housing throughout this area is of very poor quality. In the . . . section, where conditions are worst, 18 per cent of the houses sur-

National Housing Act
veyed were in very bad repair, 19 per cent had no baths, and 7 per cent were badly crowded. Interspersed with industrial buildings and bisected by the interurban tracks, this area bears all the hallmarks of a slum.
The report goes on to describe the existence of numerous cabins, waterfront shacks and house boats, and there is reference to many houses the rooms of which have no access at all to outside air. Although I will not burden the house with this, there are listed also numerous cases, which the people making the survey found, of families living in the greatest hardship and under dreadful conditions.
I want to put my view on record as strongly as I can. I am certain that we shall never solve the housing problem in the low income groups without a subsidy on housing and without the dominion government bearing part of that subsidy and taking the lead in making the arrangements necessary to get this kind of scheme in operation.

speechtext:
If I may go on, Mr. Speaker, I was saying that I am as certain as I stand here that this problem will never be solved until the dominion government takes the lead in bringing about a scheme of subsidies for low rental housing for those in the low income groups. I know that this session as well as in previous sessions, the minister has given his view against that. But I want to appeal to him again to change his mind and get after this problem. Faced as we are with the other problem of getting roofs over people's heads, there is some excuse perhaps at this moment for our not having such a scheme. But hon. members will recall that it was not until after a year of criticism and suggestions from this side of the house that the government got after the production of building materials so that we might deal with the present problem. They were a year late in realizing that necessity and getting after it. I do not want to see them a year late in promoting a scheme of low rental housing.
A programme like this cannot be developed in a minute. It requires cooperation at every level of government; it requires cooperation from citizens' committees, and it will require all sorts of work for whoever considers the setting up of a building company and getting going with the actual construction. When you think of the record of the government in bringing about any kind of agreement between the dominion and the provinces, you can visualize how they would be on the dominion, provincial and municipal level. That is why I am so anxious that they reverse their policy and make a decision to go after this now. I urge them not to be a year late again.
I am not advocating a sort of general wide-open building of houses by the dominion government for every person in Canada; far from it. All I am advocating is that cases of real need be taken care of. If we restrict any such scheme to cases of real need, the government will not have to worry about the cost which would be involved. It is not a question of making a hand-out to everyone in Canada; it is only a matter of dealing with the cases in which actual physical living conditions are now so greatly below standard as to imperil the health and the social security of the people. Any study I have made and any figures I have been given by responsible people indicate that if you tie your subsidized low rental housing scheme to slum clearance and see to it that the people you move into the houses are moved out of quarters which are unfit for human habitation, then you can keep your scheme under control and you do
National Housing Act

not let it get out of hand financially. Moreover, you have basic social security, a much better kind of social security, in my submission, than that provided by paying out cheques every month-even although measures of that kind may be necessary too. But I suggest that by this kind of scheme you are making a fundamental approach to the improvement of the health of the nation, and you are making a real contribution to the removal of juvenile delinquency. We have had one debate on that very important point, and we shall have another when we come to consider the Penitentiary Act again.
I want to give one more excerpt from this report on the contribution that would be made by a housing scheme to the solution of juvenile delinquency. Again I have actual figures obtained in this survey of a Canadian city, which will indicate what connection there is between housing conditions and juvenile crime. Again I shall not refer to the particular area. "In this area between such and such streets the average delinquency over the five years 1930-34 was fifteen delinquents per hundred of school population of comparable age as compared with under three per hundred in the outer areas of the city." I think that is a most striking example. The same report gives the costs of administration of police, social and other services in area* of the city, and it is shown that these figures are about the same in areas where housing is good, but that the costs are comparably higher in areas where housing is bad.
This matter has been discussed many times in this house, and my only reason for bringing it once more to the attention of the minister is that I feel that this is perhaps the latest time a scheme like this could be prepared and put into operation without again being late in meeting a real housing emergency. No doubt the agreement would be difficult to negotiate because three levels of government are concerned and each government would have to make some financial contribution. The proportions would have to be arrived at and of course the actual building would have to be done by a municipal or some other nonprofit housing corporation. No city or province could go into it without the dominion giving a lead, because they would not dare embark upon that kind of expenditure alone. The matter is entirely in the hands of this government to do or not to do.
I conclude by saying that it would be more than inexcusable if the government were again late in embarking upon a programme which any government in Canada is bound to carry out in the next few years.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure you that I shall take only a few minutes of the time of the house this afternoon, but I should like to make a few general observations as well as offer some earnest suggestions on this subject to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). My purpose in speaking is to draw the attention of the minister to the aspects of our housing problem which particularly affect the rural parts of the country. I feel that the government has been so busy and preoccupied with providing housing in the urban centres that it has done very little to assist in providing housing in rural parts. I know that there are difficulties to be faced, but the present legislation does provide for assistance in providing housing on farms and in rural areas.
Owing to conditions beyond our control the provisions of the act have not been applied to any extent to rural areas. They have been applied mainly to the larger towns and cities; I think I am quite right in saying that it has been found impossible to take advantage of them to build houses in the small villages and rural communities. I have analysed the act and the amendments provided by this bill and I feel sure that once he has been given these new powers the minister could carry out all the suggestions I am going to make.
The various government housing schemes which have been carried out in the last few years have been of great assistance to the cities. One needs only to go to Winnipeg or St. Boniface, to mention two cities in the central part of Manitoba, and he will see street after street of new houses which have been built in the last two or three years. That is a very happy condition and everyone who comes back to Winnipeg after having been away for a year or two notices it. It is all very well, and I rejoice with everyone else because these new houses have been built, but unfortunately this condition has had a counter-effect upon the rural parts of Manitoba.
There has been a siphoning off of people from the rural parts to the cities to a far greater extent than many realize. I suppose this is a natural consequence of the many new houses which have been built in the cities. As no houses have been built in our small villages or on the farms there is a tendency for people to move to points where houses are available. Contrary to common belief the people migrating to the cities have not been the younger people; it has been mostly older people. I know of many people who have retired from farms and instead of

National Housing Act
settling down in the village or town as they used to do in years gone by they have gone up to the city and bought a house. It is mostly these older retired people who have migrated to the city.
The provisions of this act have been taken advantage of in the larger towns and cities because the lending companies have felt that their investment was a little safer in those places and they were willing to make loans for houses. The small villages have been completely left out. In many of these villages there are no industries and the lending companies have felt that it would not be a good investment to lend money on houses. I hope that under the new amendments to the bill more assistance will be given to housing in the smaller villages. If this were done I believe that housing conditions in the cities would be alleviated. My suggestion to the minister is that more attention should be given to the small villages and unincorporated towns, as well as to the building of houses on faSrns.
Unfortunately very little has been done to promote better housing on our farms. So far the government has not even offered any suggestions to our farmers as to how they can get economical, decent and pleasant homes. I have here a booklet, containing a series of plans and designs, which was issued by the national housing administration. These plans are exclusively for homes for urban areas, although some of them could be adapted for use in larger towns. None of them could possibly fit the needs of any farmer, nor would they be suitable for homes on farms.
My further suggestion is that in order to fill that tremendous gap. to meet that pressing need, the minister at once conduct a competition in all the nine provinces to secure plans, designs and specifications for rural and, more particularly, farm housing. The minister has the power to do it. It is definitely stated in the act; all he has to do is to say the word and the thing will be done. If he does that, a great many people throughout Canada will be grateful and it will mean a service worth millions of dollars to that section of our country.
After all, in this country which is predominantly agricultural, a good third of the population are living in rural homes. There is a definite need for help, or for the giving of suggestions to the farmers, particularly when it can be done without great cost to the government, and would render such great service to all concerned.
Water is the one item which hampers housing operations in rural sections. This applies more particularly to my district,
although it has some application generally throughout western Canada. I will refer to one instance in particular. In the Red River valley water is available, but unfortunately it is so alkaline that it cannot be used for household purposes. Under the heading of research, and at little cost to the government, the minister could give a helping hand if he were to send one or two scientists out there to make a complete analysis of the water supply in that area, which serves a large number of people. I would suggest that the water be analysed to see what can be done to improve it. Many companies have claimed that they could make first-class water out of it; but my understanding is that so far the cost has been prohibitive. I am sure that with a little research means could be found of purifying the water. This would mean a good supply of pure water for, I would say, half of the province of Manitoba. And I know this problem exists in many other parts of Canada.
If more attention were directed to housing in rural areas, the housing problem in the cities would be partly solved. As I said before, migration of people from the rural parts of Manitoba to the cities has been our greatest problem. I have made it a point to discuss the matter with individuals who have migrated to the cities, and the answer I received was that in most instances they had reached the age of retirement and had turned their farms over to their sons. They pointed out that they did not feel like entering into construction operations under conditions such as exist today. So much bother and cost was involved that they simply went to the cities and bought old houses.
Hon. members know that despite the housing shortage in various cities, anyone with cash can go to a city and buy a house. In the newspapers one always sees two or three columns listing houses for sale. That is exactly what these farmers have done. Young people who would have put up houses in towns have not the resources and cannot get the necessary assistance because, as I pointed out, the act is not applicable to smaller towns. Consequently younger people are in no position to put up houses. On the other hand the older people do not feel the urge and have reached an age where they do not wish to take the responsibility of building.
The result is that the younger people take the place of the older folk, and those older folk in turn migrate to the cities. Our rural population is decreasing, while that in the cities is increasing, and this adds to the headache of both federal and provincial governments.
National Housing Act

I feel sure that if the minister will look into this matter he could render tremendous help to the people in rural areas, while at the same time give assistance to those in urban areas.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) upon the helpful contribution he has made to the debate. I share the opinions he has expressed so well with regard to rural housing in Canada. I have the doubtful honour of representing a constituency where, according to the 1941 statistics, based on such well known standards as availability of electricity, fireproof chimneys, electric lights and running water, we have the worst record in all Canada.
I have not been unmindful of the problems of the people I represent. In the past when discussing housing I have approached the problem from a broad point of view, realizing that there is not much likelihood of our solving the housing problem in Saskatchewan, and in Mackenzie constituency in particular, until we can get some machinery which will make possible modern low-cost housing all across Canada.
I am afraid I am not as optimistic as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) with regard to the usefulness of this particular bill. In the final analysis, of course, I shall support it, because it does offer some improvement. It does make it possible for direct loans to be made where at the present time it is impossible for people in many parts of Canada to take advantage of the machinery.
I should like however to devote the time at my disposal this afternoon to focusing attention on the critical situation still existing in Canada, which will not be improved by these minor changes in the National Housing Act. Indeed, if it were not for the outstanding contribution the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) made during the war, I would be pressing for his resignation, on account of the housing conditions in Canada.
I want to say however that the people of Canada, and indeed those of the united nations, will always be grateful to the minister for the imaginative way he discharged his duties during the war. I hold in my hand one of the Canadian information service publications. These are publications which are sent to other countries and which reported on Canadian achievements during the war. All hon. members can be proud of this accurate record of performance. At page 27 we find a table giving the estimated value of war productionmerchant vessels, naval vessels, aircraft, mechanical transport, armoured fighting vehicles, guns and small ammunition, small arms, chemicals, instruments, defence construction and government financed expansion. These costs are set down at a grand total of $11,501 million. Then at page 47 we find a summary of Canada's mutual aid expenditure. Again in this connection the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply must receive a good deal of credit for making available to our allies-to Australia, the British West Indies, China, France, India, New Zealand, U.S.S.R., and the United Kingdom-goods to the value of $2,575 million. This means that the minister was responsible for expenditures during the war years running over $14 billion.
All I am suggesting is that the responsible minister who was able to organize Canadian man-power and materials to such an extent, and to achieve such performance during the years of war, must be able to do better than the present development in housing would indicate.
I have another of the Canadian information service publications available in other countries which tell in a graphic way of what has been done. The minister of reconstruction is personally interested in many of these achievements. We find on page 9 pictures of the Shipshaw power development; on another page pictures of ships being 'launched; on another page pictures of shells that were manufactured, and pictures of elevators which were built by the minister before he entered public life.
I have here the white paper presented to parliament by the minister in April, 1945, and at page 14 under "Public Investment" I find this:
The post-war employment problem is not to be solved by huge expenditures on "public works." Efforts to increase and stabilize employment and income must pervade all economic policies. On the other hand, it is the firm intention of the government to institute a system of managing its capital expenditures so that they may contribute to the maximum to the improvement and stabilization of employment and income.
The white paper makes it very clear that the Liberal government of Canada in no way is to be handicapped by financial difficulties in government financing, for at page 21 it says:
In these circumstances, the government considers the post-war debt problem to be quite manageable.
There was no worrying about Canada's debt, and very few members from any part of the

National Housing Act
country took time in the budget debate to complain of Canada's national debt. The white paper goes on:
Fiscal policy during the war has necessarily been based on economic as much as purely financial consideration. It is proposed to extend that practice into the post-war years and apply war experience to the problems of peace.
If this white paper means anything, now is the time for the administration to demonstrate that its observations had application to the problem of housing. Members of the house will recall that in the debate on the address on February 7 of this year the minister gave us quite a rosy picture of the housing situation, although there were a few discordant notes in his speech. He said:
I also realize that the accomplishment of a target is dependent upon the ability of the Canadian people to absorb new housing at the present level of building costs. Further, the need for housing is so great that any target should be set at the very limit of possible accomplishment. In 1947 we will be making a vigorous effort to meet a target of 80.000 residential units.
Further on he said:
As in 1946, we will continue to rely for the major portion of our new housing upon private endeavour. It is our policy to ensure that as much new housing as possible be built by private initiative. Towards this end we will lend every facility. If, however, for any reason the supply of housing by private initiative is insufficient, then and then only will the dominion government take a direct position in the housing field. I have already dealt with a number of operations in which the dominion is already participating for this reason. We would be very happy to withdraw from these activities, but, at the present time, this much needed type of housing would not be produced by other means.
That speech was delivered in the house on February- 7. On May 15 the Ottawa Journal, under the heading "Government concurs with dropping of Ottawa housing, says Howe" carries this story:
The 1946 programme now- is well advanced, and it is apparent that practically every project will exceed the "target" price, and that correspondingly high rentals will result.
It had been originally anticipated that rentals might be of the order of $35 to $40 for four-room units. Because of increased building costs, rentals calculated upon the formula are considerably higher.
Even in the 1946 programme it would be extremely difficult to meet the rental level originally anticipated.
These comments were made at the time the announcement was made that Housing Enterprises Limited was abandoning plans for a S3,000,000 apartment project along Mann avenue in Ottawa and a similar undertaking
amounting to $1,500,000 in Toronto. The Ottawa project was to house 408 families and the Toronto project another 200.
Recently I have received a report on the number of building permits issued in January, February and March of 1946 as compared with 1947. It is significant that there is a marked falling off in the first three months of 1947 as compared with 1946. In 1947, 4,807 building permits were issued for dwelling units, as compared with 5,512 in 1946. The reports from all parts of Canada indicate that there are not going to be buyers for a much longer period for houses selling at present prices.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that only a very small percentage of Canadian families are in a position to pay a monthly rental of S50 or more or to buy houses at prevailing costs. An analysis of taxation statistics published by the Department of National Revenue shows that there are only 183,318 taxpayers in Canada with an income of $3,000 or more. A rent of $50 a month is what might reasonably be expected from this group. Another 126,900 taxpayers receive from $2,500 to $3,000. They could afford to pay $45 a month, or if they were prepared to increase their rent payments and get along with older clothing and pass up the medical and educational expenses they would normally make they might be able to pay $50 a month. Those two groups total 310,218. They include single taxpayers with no dependents.	[DOT]
There are 293,500 making from $2,000 to $2,500. They could afford to pay $36.50 per month, on the assumption that one-fifth of one's income should go for housing. There are 903,930 taxpayers and non-taxpayers making between $1,000 and $2,000 a year. They cannot afford to pay more than $25 a month. There are 345,400 married men earning under $1,000 a year, and they cannot afford to pay more than $12 a month rent. So you see, Mr. Speaker, we have more than a million families who must find housing at $25 a month or less, and 345,000 who are getting so little income that $12 is the maximum they should plan for shelter.
In view of these statistics it cannot be denied that we have almost reached the saturation point in disposing of housing built at present prices in Canada. The situation throughout Canada is the same. I have received a copy of a letter which went to the Prime Minister from the Citizens' Housing and Planning Association of Toronto. I assume that all members received a copy of this letter. The chairman of the committee is
National Housing Act

Mr. Clark, the vice-chairman Mrs. Luffman, and the secretary, Mrs. Donald Fraser. I am not acquainted with any of these people, but the committee comprises quite an impressive list of persons. In the committee's letter to the Prime Minister some caustic comments are made regarding Canada's housing situation. They say:
The housing policy of your government may be summed up in three points:
(1)	Belief that private enterprise can and will build a sufficient supply of rental housing for Canadians. This conviction has been repeatedly asserted by Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Howe in parliament. It is contrary to the findings of your own experts in the Curtis report; it is contrary to the experience of every other country, and hence has been consistently opposed by this organization.
(2)	Opposition to public housing authorities, as expressed in the interpretation of the National Housing Act by Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Howe, and only recently modified for Toronto.
(3)	Denial of federal responsibility for a public housing programme, alleging this to be primarily a provincial responsibility.
It is pertinent to look at the Canadian situation in the light of this policy, and the recent decision of housing enterprises.
(1)	The failure of housing enterprises to achieve rental housing plainly disproves the claim that private enterprise will build rental housing for the middle income group. Private enterprise was not interested in building such housing and considerable pressure has to be exerted by your government on the insurance companies to bring them into this field. Now they give up and say it cannot be done. Valuable time and effort have been spent to prove what was clear at the outset-that housing for a large section of our population has to be public housing.
(2)	If we are to have public housing, we need municipal (or regional) housing authorities, as in England and in the United States. These must be allowed for and encouraged by the federal policy.
(3)	The government of Canada can no longer evade responsibility for a positive policy of housing for Canadians. The need is national and urgent; many of the factors in creating it and meeting it are a national responsibility. Leadership and planning on a national scale are essential and urgent; the provinces are neither equipped nor prepared to operate in this field. Denial of federal responsibility only postpones action still further; some provinces could not act at all, and the cross-country picture would be one of gaps, unequal standards, delay, and confusion; of this we have had too much already. A clear national policy is required to meet this national domestic emergency.
Thousands of good Canadian families are trying to live under desperate housing conditions-in tents, in trailers, in factory buildings, stores and shacks of all kinds. Local health authorities have virtually ceased to try to enforce sanitary conditions in thousands of dwellings, clearly unfit for human occupancy, but crowded with hard-pressed Canadian families. Welfare authorities are at their wits' end to house the families daily being evicted.
The security of family life in Canada is gravely affected. Our divorce rate is rising, and 
authorities, lay and church alike, are alarmed at the causes. Housing is a common one. A young family today faces great difficulties and the lack of housing contributes to them. It is a hazard we can reduce by resolute policy and effective action. Further drift in the matter is a direct contribution by government to the further undermining of Canadian family life.
I submit, to hon. members that this is a fair description of the situation in Canada. I must remind the house that the committee is not describing a new situation, not one that has been created by the war. I hold in my hand the report of the lieutenant governor's committee on housing conditions in Toronto, 1934. It is interesting to note that such well known persons as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who was then the general manager of the National Trust Company, president of the Board of Trade of Toronto and chairman of the board of trustees of Queen's university, -was a member of that committee. The report, which I am sure is well known to most hon. members who have made a study of housing, contains a disgraceful picture of what is commonly known as Toronto the good, a description of the ward; pictures of the back yards there. There is a description of the housing shortage and a section on slums, a section on sanitation, a section on food storage, tuberculosis, infant mortality, juvenile delinquency, crime and family life. I submit that it is a very serious reflection on a great country, a great province and a proud city such as Toronto to have a report of this sort submitted in the year 1934, and now so many years later conditions are virtually unchanged. The same sort of report could be presented today in spite of the fact that Toronto is the second city in the dominion. Huge sums were subscribed for our war effort. Surely the people of this country can evolve a programme that will clear away the slums, that will build modern bouses and improve the living conditions of the people of that area.
I hold in my hand a picture from Vancouver which has a heading, "Low rental homes or swimming pools. Vancouver has double-crossed its homeless war veterans". Here is a picture of Vancouver's disgraceful housing conditions on the one side and on the'other a picture of a privately owned swimming pool which is being installed in one of the residential areas of that city. The failure of the federal government to retain some of their controls, to decide what is essential and what is not essential material makes it possible for people who live in one part of the city to use tight material and short labour to provide a swimming pool when they have the great ocean available for swimming at least for many months of the year, while other people

National Housing Act
have to live in the sort of housing conditions so well described in the report read by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt).
The last report of the chief inspector of the sanitation and housing division of the city of Winnipeg repeats the information that has been given by the health department of Winnipeg year after year. On page 5 I find a table showing the unlawful emergency occupa-lion of certain premises as dwellings. From that, table I find that there are twenty-three families living in stores; thirteen families in garages, one in tourist cabins, nine in unfinished dwellings and attics; twelve in cellars; one in a stable and one in a church. There are seventy-eight children in the group who were found to be living in emergency occupation. unlawful occupation. The health authorities of the city point out that it is intolerable that people should be living under these conditions, but it is a question of living there or living out under the sky, which is not so desirable in Winnipeg, certainly in the winter months. We find that there are 16.000 families who made application for accommodation in Winnipeg in 1946. Only eight per cent were able to be accommodated. Some very useful recommendations are made by the chief inspector, but the conclusion is significant:
House hungry squatters have not so far appeared in this city, but let us not be complacent about this. All that is needed is the spark, a leader, and we are likely then to have some rude experiences. The labour, money and material bottlenecks were broken during the war. The same bottlenecks have come to life again in this, the post-war period. The force or power that broke the bottleneck of war supplies was the federal government, acting presumably by the will of the people of this country. This power, so effective for war purposes, is now apparently atrophied and useless, indicating unmistakably the indifference or apathy of the general public and certain of the politicians, to a situation that should cause them serious concern.
So much for Winnipeg. I have here a picture from the Montreal Gazette of May 8, which has the heading:	"Family of eight,
with sick baby and money to pay rent, evicted." Underneath the photograph the following appears:	"Family evicted from
north-end home." Here is a picture of the law officers and the family with two little children in arms who have no rooms to which to go. That took place in the great and wealthy city of Montreal.
In the Ottawa Journal of Tuesday of this week appears a story:	"Low rental housing
project proposed by Ottawa committee." In the article it says:
Hr. Goodfellow told of fifty-nine families that had to be broken up because there was no room for the children.
"The problem is growing daily," Mr. Good-fellow said. "Unless we get some homes I don't know what might happen this fall." Mr. Pickering raised the question whether it was the responsibility of the committee to continue working on housing. "I think it is the responsibility of this committee to shove the responsibility exactly where it belongs-on the shoulders of the city of Ottawa, central mortgage, private enterprise and labour," he asserted.
In the meantime men who fought for their country and who were assured that when the war was over nothing would be too good for them are finding it next to impossible to find shelter. Just the other day I was talking to a man who was still in the army and who bought a new house in Ottawa. He was desperate. The only place that he was able to find for his wife and baby was this house. I understand the price paid was $9,800. What chance has a man on army pay to meet monthly payments on a $9,800 house. Yet this house is not any better than a house in which a veteran should live, and I am sure in normal times it could be built for $5,000 or less. We cannot ask these young men who were able to use a $100,000 tank or a $250,000 plane to live in the hovels that are available, the only places that are available in many of these cities. I understand that just this week the mayor of Hull came out urging that something be done by the dominion government to provide low-cost public housing. I am sure that those of us who spend the taxpayers' money must take notice of the conditions which exist in the country.
The bureau of statistics, in analysing the statistics compiled in the 1941 census, compares housing conditions in Ottawa and Hull just across the river. We find that in Hull 34 per cent of the houses are crowded as compared with 17 per cent in Ottawa. The value of home ownership in Hull is $2,300 as compared with $4,600 in Ottawa. Monthly rentals are much higher of course in Ottawa, and the households with exclusive use of bathing facilities represent 43 per cent in Hull and 84 per cent in Ottawa. Households with four conveniences-radio, telephone, vacuum cleaner and running water-are 4.7 in Hull as compared with 27 in Ottawa.
I submit that while we have people, in this day and age, who live in cities where there is central heating, where there are modern conveniences, it is a matter of real concern to the nation and to parliament to find these conditions. This brings me to the point mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, which should be developed. I think the only solution is for this government to . recognize that at least one third of the people in Canada simply have no chance of getting
National Housing Act

housing under the legislation at present on our statute books; and further, that if the federal government does not give a lead, if it does not evolve policies which have not yet been evolved, we are going into a depression and we are not going to have a housing programme to provide a guarantee that there will be useful employment and a market for many materials.
In the United States they made a study which indicates that in 1939 19-9 per cent of the gross national product was used in housing. They came to the conclusion that in the two years before the 1929 depression, if they had faced the facts and realized that the falling off of housing construction was one signal indicating that they were headed for depression, and if something had been done with a view to working out a housing programme such as was worked out in Great Britain or Sweden, they could have prevented the depression having the impact it did.
I find in one of the "Housing Abroad" series published by the minister, volume 1, No. 1, a chart showing what happened to housing and the national income in Canada, Great Britain and the United States. In Great Britain, where they decided to carry out slum clearing and a low-rental housing programme, there was a rather slight drop in the national income, and they actually increased the number of houses built during that period. But in Canada there was a falling off in the number of houses being built before there was any indication that we were headed for a slump. By the time we got down to the bottom, however, in 1934 we were down to 16 points as compared with 100 in 1929, in house building. The same thing happened to a lesser degree in the United States; and now, as the falling off in building permits and the folding up of the programme under housing enterprises would indicate, we have reached the saturation point in Canada in disposing of houses under present terms. Now therefore is the time when the government should face the question of a subsidized low-cost housing programme as part of our post-war undertakings. If we could undertake that kind of programme immediately and enlist the cooperation of the provinces and the municipalities, I am sure it would be a major factor in preventing the depression from reducing our standard of living, as happened during the last depression.
In another publication with regard to manpower and material requirements for a housing programme, I find that to carry out a programme of 80,000 houses in a year it would require 403 million man hours; and on a rough calculation, using the basis of SI per hour, 
there is an expenditure of over $400 million. There is also the list of materials used in the
80.000	houses unit, such as cement, bricks, tiles, lumber products, lath and plaster, roofing, paint, plumbing facilities, electrical equipment, glass, and so on, totalling $280 million. In other words, for less than one billion dollars, 80,000 houses could be built. In view of the fact that the minister during the war was able to spend over thirteen billions, representing man-power and material, surely this modest programme that has been outlined of
80.000	houses a year can be realized.
We propose therefore to move certain amendments as we discuss the clauses and we would like to introduce a preamble which would set out our Canadian objective, just as has been done in Australia and the United States. We suggest it be the objective of this parliament to provide a programme of housing for the Canadian people which would ensure a separate home in a good neighbourhood for every family that desires one. We must accept the principle that society has reached the stage where a house of good quality properly equipped is not only the need but the right of every citizen. Where a family cannot own such a house, it is the duty of the state to bridge the gap by a rental subsidy.
We also think it should be the objective, in realizing this principle, to provide for the replacement of slums and other substandard housing in rural areas, to obviate overcrowding and facilitate progress in an orderly manner towards a proper standard of housing for the entire Canadian people. Another objective is the systematic planning of cities and neighbourhoods so as to develop and redevelop communities, which will provide good surroundings for home life and adequate facilities for advancing the industrial and cultural welfare of the nation.
Consideration in undertaking the large scale housing programme envisaged by the act should be given to the undeniable fact that a stable level of construction throughout the years immediately ahead is one of the most necessary factors in ensuring a steady level of employment, which in turn would provide buying power essential to prosperity at home and abroad. '
I submit that if the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is not now prepared to take steps different from those that he has followed in the past he is going to be responsible for one of the most serious conditions we have witnessed in Canada, because we cannot expect Canadian citizens indefinitely, in view of our remarkable performance during the war, to be told that we have not now the ways and

National Housing Act
means of solving a little problem such as diverting a billion dollars' worth of man-power and material into the housing business each year.
I am not suggesting that all this should be spent under public housing. I think our expenditures could be divided roughly into three groups. One-third of our people will be able to build dwellings without assistance from anyone; one-third will be in the middle group who will need to take advantage of the facilities afforded by Central Mortgage and Housing, people in the middle income groups; and one-third of the people must be provided for by public low-cost housing, which will be built only if the federal government is prepared to guarantee that the necessary subsidy will be paid to bridge the gap between what the individual can pay and what is the economic rent to provide these services.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a few remarks on this bill as it. is proposed to be amended. It is unlikely that anything new can be said in regard to the summary of conditions which such legislation should endeavour to meet. The previous speaker has placed on record a wealth of data which cannot help but impress those who have been listening. Everyone in this house will agree without question that the housing situation is desperate, and I am going to be critical of the government's policy in that regard. In doing so, of course I want to say that I have not the slightest doubt that the right hon. gentleman who administers this legislation has great capacity. He is a competent administrator, and if the results are not as we desire them, or as I believe it is quite possible to make them, I do not think the minister individually is to blame. He has been limited by the system under which he is working. His hands have been tied by practices and methods which cannot meet the situation. I hope that, after the discussion which is now going on with respect to this matter, the minister will take the bit in his teeth and do for peace what he did for war.
As I have said, the results are unsatisfactory, and that is putting it mildly. The bill which is now before us amends the previous legislation in the first place, by reducing the amount of the initial payment required to be made by the borrower who intends to build a house. In the second place, it extends the period of amortization to thirty years. In the third place, it brings duplex houses within the benefits of the act. Of course these are all minor improvements. Personally, I welcome them. So far as they go, and they do
not go very far, I am for them; I am going to vote for that legislation. But I suggest, sir, that no possible amendment to this act could make it accomplish what the necessity of the moment demands that it should accomplish. I question whether anything short of an entirely new objective, an entirely new purpose, an entirely new piece of legislation, can possibly do the job. The chief purpose of this act appears as set forth in section 1 of the bill:
... to protect the mortgage security the said lending institution and the corporation may join in making supplementary joint loans to the borrower and in taking such other measures and steps as may be required in accordance with normal mortgage practice to safeguard the interests of His Majesty and the said lending institution.
I have no doubt that this legislation will protect His Majesty. I have no doubt that it will protect the lending institution. But it should protect the homeless people of Canada. That is the essential purpose which is lacking in this legislation, and that is the burden of the criticism which I want to make with respect to it.
There are three criticisms of the housing policy of the government which I should like to emphasize. In the first place, there are not nearly enough houses being built.

I am now discussing the legislation which is before us and do not wish to complicate the matter by taking up other schemes.
In the next place, the cost of houses now being built is so high as to be out of the
National Housing Act

reach of more than two-thirds of the entire population of Canada. I happen to be living in a six-room house which was bought last week from the contractor at $9,500.

speechtext: Your house?

speechtext:
No, it is not my house; I am renting a room in it. It has been estimated-if I mistake not, by the previous minister of finance-that building a house will cost at least $1,000 a room. I think that is a conservative estimate. I say next, sir, that the average family of five needs a house of eight rooms; so that even if we accept the estimate of 81,000 a room, an eight-room house, which the average family of five needs, would cost $8,000 to build. Let me make an estimate of what such a house, under the present set-up, will cost the purchaser. I am taking into account the repayment of the principal and the interest, and the amortization scheme. I am taking into account also annual taxes and am estimating them at only $100 a year; and I think that is low. I am taking into account that annual insurance will cost about $13, at the rate of fifty cents per 100 for three years. There should be a depreciation of $200 a year for forty years of the life of the dwelling. That would mean a monthly payment of $66.42, which in thirty years would amount to $23,911.20. That is a figure far beyond the limitations of the financial ability of the average working man in this country. It means that he would have to put into the building of his home a proportion of his income so great as to impair the living of his family and himself in many essential requirements. The bill provides that a certain amount may be borrowed under certain conditions; on an $8,000 dwelling, 95 per cent of the first $3,000, 85 per cent of the next $3,000, and 70 per cent of the remainder may be borrowed.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) pointed out in his budget speech, and this has been emphasized a number of times during the budget debate, that over half of the working people of Canada do not receive a sufficient income to be taxable under the income tax scheme. The exemption figure for a married man with a family of two is $1,700. I think it is clear that no man with a family receiving less than $2,500 could ever think of building a home under the present scheme with any hope of ever paying for that home. All you have to do is to think about the possibility of a week or two of sickness, a month or two or six months of unemployment, or some other calamity and you realize that the interest begins to pile up, the principal is

unpaid and you begin to go behind. That may be repeated until the payments cannot be made in thirty years; your children's children will have to finish paying and nothing but the ashes of the home will be left when the payments are completed. I suggest that those who accept the present arrangement will feel that they are compelled to take it. It will be a case of necessity, and not their wills consenting.
I agree with the hon. member who preceded me that the greatest need is for a scheme of low-rental houses. Possibly these could be built by public bodies and rented to individuals at a rate which would cover the replacement cost of the building in, say forty years. Whatever was the estimated life of the building, the rental cost should be spread over that number of years, so that when the building is no longer useful it will have been paid for and the money available to build the next one, Such a scheme is perfectly sound because there is no danger of loss.
There is no reason why a better method of financing than the one now suggested could not be devised. I want to register my opposition to the method of financing which has been adopted by the government and which appears in the present legislation. It may be presumed that eventually we shall catch up with the shortages in building material, but there is no man who will live long enough to catch up with four and a half per cent. That just cannot be done, and there is no use in thinking it can be done. If he is not in the low-income class he will not borrow; he will build his house and save the four and a half per cent, which would be the wiser thing for him to do,
I am going to suggest that the government devise a new scheme to provide homes at low rentals for the people of Canada. These homes could be built in a manner similar to that adopted for the great undertakings in the war period which were supervised by the right hon. gentleman who will be administering this legislation. We plunged into tremendous expenditures for war. All the materials that were created by our finance and our efforts were blown to hell and we were left with nothing but a debt. Here we are suggesting that for peace purposes the government undertake a constructive scheme for the building of homes which will leave the nation with an asset equal to every dollar that is put into it. Why there should be any hesitancy in proceeding to build the houses required is utterly beyond me.
I am going to suggest that we use the national credit to finance this housing scheme. Not only do I suggest that we use it for

National Housing Act
housing, but if I had the time I should like to suggest and do more than suggest that we use it for the establishment of new industries and for the provision of additional capital equipment for older industries which need to be brought up to date.

speechtext:
If I had been checked up every time I have departed from the paths of righteousness as quickly as Your Honour has now checked me up I would have been a much better man. I shall not go beyond merely suggesting that I am not confining my proposal of national financing to the one project. However I am going to confine it to the one project as you have just suggested. The mechanism for doing this would be quite stereotyped. There is no need for any mythical scheme to be conjured up. It is easily understood how these things are done and how easily they can be set up. I suggest that it is the responsibility of the Minister of Finance, under the guidance of the government, to provide such mechanism. It can be operated through the Bank of Canada, and perhaps it might be found necessary to set up a crown company to carry out the building of the houses required. But the main thing is that we can well afford to finance any real asset we are competent to create. In fact we cannot afford not to finance any enterprise in which necessity urges us to engage. And, as I have already said, every home built under such a scheme would represent a national asset equal to the amount of money expended in its building. So that there is no risk whatsoever. There is none to be incurred.
But that is not so now. Under the present scheme the government takes all the risk and the financial corporations take all the interest. It seems to be a sort of priorities field of investment for insurance companies, at a rate of interest which would be very difficult to get at the present time anywhere else, and with safety guarantees unequalled anywhere, any time.
The government might begin to launch such a scheme in a more or less orthodox way. If it is true that we are now experiencing an inflationary condition in Canada, there is no reason why the government should not sell bonds to build houses, and take up the surplus cash floating around so that it might be used to take care of the greatest need of the nation at the present time. That would be a perfectly orthodox procedure. If there are interest moneys paid, it would go to the people who bought the bonds, namely the people of Canada in general. If it were financed in any other way, and if interest were charged,
the money would go into the public treasury and would not pass into the hands of private individuals. While money is plentiful, the financing could be done by issuing bonds.
I do not think that is the best way to do it; but since we cannot be expected to break away from orthodoxy overnight, that would be one way to do it; and it would be better than not doing it. I suggest that it be done in that way, since that is the only way of doing it that the government would be likely to consider, and that we should lend to home builders the money required, at the cost of administration. It would not be long until monthly rentals from such houses would begin to come in. After a while, all new houses would be built from moneys collected as rentals from those already built and in operation.
But when money is scarce, as it is likely to be after the inflation is over, these houses would be available. We must remember that there is always the drop backwards. We have never had a boom without its corresponding slump, and I doubt whether we shall have any different experience this time because I have heard no scheme advanced for preventing the usual thing from happening. I expect, therefore, that the usual will happen; and it will happen because the profits which have been siphoned off by the profit-takers of the nation have not been reinvested quickly enough to be paid out in wages, and thus to keep the flow of purchasing power running in balance.
When this happens it would be a good thing for the government to do what our hon. friends here are asking.

That is what the banks would do, if we borrowed from them; and there is no reason why we should not do it in: a direct way ourselves, without interest. It could be done by the payment of only administration costs. That would check the deflationary tendency following a boom, although it would not be a cure. It would help the economic system as a whole.
I conclude by saying that, although the minister is a gentleman of much greater experience than I am in matters of administration and of government, he might do well if at least he were to take some notice of the ideas which hon. members have tried to present in respect of this great problem of housing. He knows as well as we do that the situation is serious; perhaps he knows much better than we do. No doubt he receives more
National Housing Act

letters about it, because he is face to face with the problem. He knows that not enough houses are being built, and knows perfectly well that the average working man cannot buy the houses being built under the present scheme. I am asking him to consider the possibility of devising a housing scheme which would make available low-rental houses, that such a scheme be financed upon the credit of the state, and at cost, and that we proceed to do it and continue in our endeavour until every Canadian family has a home.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly concerning the expression used by the preceding speaker- "the necessity of the moment", and I wish to address myself to those words.
Before doing so, however, I should like to refer to the observations of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), who spoke about Toronto and outlined some of the unfortunate housing conditions in that city. I am sure the hon. member will be glad to know that the city council, welfare institutions and all other agencies in the city have made every effort to meet the housing shortage. Last winter, although they passed through several critical periods, they did manage to keep a roof over everyone's head. Among other things, they reconverted Trinity Barracks and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars outside the city limits in the development of water and road services in the county of York in connection with housing developments in that area.
My one brief suggestion to the minister would be that, in company with the rentals administration of the government, he consider lifting the freezing orders on new accommodation opened after a certain date. I do not mean that the rentals administration order as it now stands should be changed, if the government insists upon retaining it. Bui I do suggest that if the government will consider lifting the freezing order and evictions order on new accommodation opened after, let us say, July 1, there will be a tremendous improvement in respect of the housing shortage in urban centres of Canada.
The minister has had the problem fully and ably presented to him. I am sure that has been done in his department, as it has been again in the house today, particularly in the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt). Mine is an urban constituency, with very small space available for further building. It is overcrowded, almost as bad in that respect as the constituency of Spadina, which is represented in this house by a Liberal member. This situation is found not only in Toronto, but in almost every

other city in Canada. It is our "immediate necessity", and I think the freezing order should be lifted on new accommodation by the first of July. By lifting it early this summer, any difficulties which may arise, administrative or personal, could be ironed out before the extremely critical period of next winter, and I am sure the minister will agree with me that next winter the housing accommodation in Canada will be extremely critical. So. Mr. Speaker, with this brief suggestion and mindful of the tremendous amount of work that lies before the house I take my seat after urging the minister to consult with the rentals administration on the suggestion I have made to him this afternoon.
