speechtext:
I shall be glad to. Recently
I attended a public meeting in Toronto at which all the difficulties, shortages of building materials, rising costs, labour difficulties and every other kind of difficulty facing builders were put before the meeting, and I was impressed with the facts given. When the minister announced to the house the other day that Housing Enterprises Limited had had to abandon some very large projects I knew he was faced with the same building difficulties. At that meeting a lot of prominent citizens advised me- and I believe they spoke with certain knowledge-that if the minister would lift the freezing order on new accommodation rented after a certain date, literally hundreds of people in every urban centre would be able to obtain accommodation. These would include veterans with families, single persons seeking rooms and perhaps board, and perhaps even large civilian families would find accommodation if the owners could be sure that their tenants, if objectionable, could be evicted. Eviction might be necessary in only five per cent or less of the new accommodation provided, and what I am asking is that the other ninety-five per cent who could be accommodated in this way should be given the chance to secure this accommodation. The real reason why people will not open their homes today is that they are afraid of having undesirable tenants come into their homes and be unable to get rid of them.
Mr. HAROLD W. TIMMINS (Parkdale): Mr. Speaker, the minister in bringing down the amendments in Bill No. 176 reminded the house that extensive amendments had been made to the National Housing Act in 1946, but that by reason of changed conditions

National Housing Act
further amendments were necessary in 1947. For the most part there seems to be a good deal of merit in the amendments. The minister proposes, for instance, in respect of national housing mortgages, that the lending value shall be increased, that there may be larger loans. In the second place, the amendments will bring about lower down-payments by purchasers which the minister said was necessary because there is less money in the hands of purchasers at this time. Further, in order that the monthly payments may be kept down to the ability of people to pay, he proposes that the loans be amortized over a period of thirty instead of twenty-five years. All these amendments are good in a sense. They do make it easier for builders to finance. But as a matter of fact, as the minister himself stated, the problems in respect to building in 1947 are not so much financial as they are physical. I do not know of a single builder or a single person who wants a house who has been unable to get a house built by reason of not being able to finance a loan. The loan does not have to be under the National Housing Act, because there are many other kinds of mortgages that one can get. So I do not believe that difficulty in financing is stopping any house building today.
We know there are four groups of house building which are in a sense government controlled and Which are looked after under the system of priority of building materials.
In presenting this bill to the house, the minister had this to say, at page 2660 of Hansard:
We propose that where there is some control on the end sale price of the house to the home owner, the ratio of loan on a $3,000 lending value shall be 95 per cent, grading down to 90 per cent on a $6,000 lending value.
I take it from that-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that he is referring there to integrated housing, because that is the only kind of housing in Canada that I know of in which the government takes any part in controlling the sale price of the house. I am pointing out to the minister, without disparaging the amendments he proposes, or minimizing the results he hopes to attain, that as a matter of fact, according to a recent return which I received from his department, only 1.691 integrated housing units were started in 1946-47. So, while the amendment which the minister proposes is to some extent proper and will bring some relief, I do not believe that the relief we shall obtain will put us very much ahead in the matter of housing accommodation. I would be prepared to gamble that housing accommodation will not be increased by more than one or two per
cent by the changes which are proposed with respect to these mortgages. Of course, when you lend up to ninety-five per cent of the value of the property you are looking for trouble. We have had experience in days gone by when mortgages were made up to fifty and sixty and seventy per cent of the value of the property, but when you get up to ninety and ninety-five per cent you are putting the purchaser in a precarious position with respect to stability and the future holding of his property. However, it may be necessary that something along this line should be done. I am only pointing out that a dangerous practice is growing up.
The minister said that conditions have changed since the last amendments to the act were made. Even since this bill was brought down on the first of May-and now it is the 29th of May-many more serious changes in conditions have taken place. In the first place, so far as integrated housing is concerned there has been some hesitation by veterans in some parts of the country to buy houses under that scheme. We also know that, so far as Housing Enterprises Limited are concerned. they have dropped their projects in at least three cities. From a return which I received on March 31. I find that at the present, time Housing Enterprises Limited are carrying on projects in some twenty-three cities. I suggest to the minister that economic conditions in respect of building are probably no different in the other parts of Canada from what they are in Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto where these projects have been stopped.
Press reports tell us that because these projects are not to be continued in Toronto, some twenty thousand units which would otherwise have been provided will not be provided. I have read with a great deal of interest the comments which have been made by Brigadier Storms with respect to the obstacles which he found in housing. If there is any man who could get through a difficulty in housing or in any other matter it is Brigadier Storms. He is not easily stopped. He was my commanding officer in France during a considerable period of the first great war. I do not know of any man who commands more ability to get things done than Brigadier Storms.
One other feature of the amendment which I should like to touch on briefly is the amendment which appears on page 2661 of Hansard, about which the minister said:
We will he seeking authority for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to convey property which it is administering for the crown. We have in mind particularly Wartime Housing units which are being sold to tenants.
National Housing Act

Wartime housing was essentially and primarily provided for veterans. The houses that I have seen and inspected in various parts of the country have no cellars under them. I do not believe it is good business for this government or for any government to sell to veterans houses without any cellars under them, because it means that in the future these people will have to live in housing units which are heated by stoves or by gas or by whatever [DOT]the local amenities may be. I do not believe that is proper housing for soldiers to have except as an expedient for the moment and temporary. I am not criticizing the government for what they have done in providing Wartime Housing. I am simply saying that some other form of ensuring the veteran his property might more properly be developed, because I do not believe that any of us should be a party to turning over to the veteran something which we know in the long run will be very much of an impediment or a detriment to him.
Turning for a moment to the next part of the act which has to do with the advent of the lending companies and the insurance companies into the field of providing scope for the development of land for building purposes, may I say that that particular venture has a good deal of merit to it. After all, we know, and the minister probably knows better than any of us, that in the larger cities practically all the land for building purposes is used up, and as you get into the townships and the municipalities you run into the difficulty of the lack of public utilities. For instance, it would be useless for a scheme to be developed miles away from schools, or miles away from water or without proper sewage facilities; and it will take a good deal of money to promote these land ventures.
Having regard to the projects which may be entered into, I should like to suggest to the minister that perhaps the department could give some leadership in seeing that in a sense these projects take the form of decentralizing communities. If I may use an illustration, surrounding Toronto on the north are three or four municipalities, Thornhill, Richmond Hill, Aurora and Newmarket. In planning these projects, one should bear in mind that perhaps suburban life is superior to urban life in so far as bringing up children and families are concerned. I am of the opinion that these projects should be developed around communities which already exist.
In the past, experience has shown that companies subdividing and promoting * land ventures have come to a disastrous end. I

know of few throughout the Dominion of Canada that have really made a success of land ventures and come through with much of their money at the end of the time when they have their land sold. The work of developing these ventures includes surveying the land. They have to have the plan passed by the municipal authorities and by the provincial planning board. They have to plan recreation and park land and also arrange for the laying in of water, sewers, pavement and sidewalks.
The minister has told us-and I think the act provides for it-that the remuneration which will pass to those who are planning these projects will be in the neighbourhood of two per cent. If I understood the minister correctly, I think he said that if there were anything over the two per cent it would have to be returned to the crown. That strikes me as a very low amount for a venture of this kind, and for that reason I have been looking for a nigger in the woodpile in respect of how the costs are going to mount and where those who will venture the funds in the particular projects will receive their remuneration. I presume the minister will not allow large sums of money to be used in these projects for administration purposes. I can see that it will be quite easy for a huge administration to be set up in the way of an office, with secretaries, draftsmen, surveyors and a great number of other people who would in a sense run the administration high, which would, of course, all be added to the costs which, in the long run, the government might have to take over and pay.
There is this other thing to be looked at, and it has happened before. Before the lending company or the insurance company gets into the project, somebody has intervened and has become the owner of the property, and that has happened in a month or two or in a week or two before the project goes through.
I suggest to the minister that some safeguards should be put in these projects so that they will not end up with this sort of thing going on. The remuneration to those who will be carrying on these projects will be small for the amount of work they will have to do.
I understand that in the United States some of the large lending companies have already gone into this field, but I am told that the remuneration they receive is in the neighbourhood of 4-5 per cent and 4-7 per cent in respect of the money venture in the project.
It seems to me that these amendments will not go nearly far enough; in fact they will not go any distance at all in solving the housing problems of Canada. They are all expedi-

National Housing Act
'ents. blit they all miss the mark, and the mark is that we have not a housing programme in Canada. All the projects which the department has worked out have been predicated for the most part on the priority system; in other words, the channeling of building material into a few hands who can in a sense control the kind of building that the government considers we should have. I think the government has missed the boat in that respect, because the statistics show-and we have used them before-that less than 12,000 homes were helped by the priority system in 1946, and according to the figures which we now have before us, we are going to be in a much worse position this year.
For instance, a release from the labour department of May 27 shows that construction contracts, mainly for home building, were down $23 million in April, 1947, compared with the corresponding period last year. No improvement was expected. According to the report, commercial construction showed little variation over last year, with the bulk of the decline showing in respect of certain industrial classes.
The minister and his department must take the responsibility in these matters. After all, some of us who have had some experience in housing think the measures which have been taken to date are not going far enough and we are really in a sense standing still. We point out to the minister, who has heard it many times before, that he must do something about the channeling of building material, in the sense that he has to call a halt to the business of so much material going into nonessential building, having regard to the fact that our primary problem today is housing for our people.
If, as a matter of fact, building costs have gone as high as they have, so high that the ordinary builder is stifled-and he built 48,000 homes last year in spite of priorities and everything else-and if, as a matter of fact, the minister is not prepared to say that home building shall get its share of material, then he and the department must assume the responsibility. One of the responsibilities he has to take is the fact that in the large cities, with the money received from the federal government, and the help of municipalities, for which I give them full credit, our people are living in conditions which are degrading and which will do a great deal in creating a demoralizing effect on the future of the nation.
We know that people are living in converted military barracks, in a converted air station barracks; they are living in buildings which formerly were munitions factories; the last
project represents one that was formerly an engineering plant. These people have to use communal accommodations; in other words, washrooms together, public rooms together; and their children are mixed up in various compartments of the same housing unit. The people there are beginning to feel that in a sense they are wards of the countiy, that provision has been made for them now and that provision will be made for them again. That is contrary to the concept which Canadians have of our people. We feel that we should be able to stand on our own feet and make our own way, but we are demoralizing the people by permitting these conditions to continue.
Part II of the National Housing Act is a useful section. It has not been used to any great extent up to this time. In Toronto, when I was on the council, we started the Regent Park project for the purpose of clearing out a slum area and providing adequate and proper accommodation for the people there.
I	have visited the district myself and I must say I was ashamed of the conditions under which the people were living there. I know that the project was a necessary one, and within the last year the minister has seen fit to place the stamp of approval on the undertaking in the Regent Park district in Toronto. That is only a beginning. I believe that part
II	of the National Housing Act must be used and used quickly for those people who, in our own country, are displaced people. Something must be done for them.
The city of Toronto cannot carry the cost alone-I am dealing with the Regent Park project at the moment-but must have help from the province because, as a matter of fact, the provinces all have their planning boards, and these matters require some provincial assistance. In addition to that, they require a great deal of federal assistance, because, if people live in a group that cannot pay the economic lent, then we the people, as my hon. friend the member for Vancouver-Burrard put it, through the governments of various levels must all take our part in providing the necessary housing.
I predict that the minister will find, with building conditions continuing as they are at the moment, that something will have to be done along these lines, within the next couple of months, I would say, because I do not believe that the various municipalities will be able to cope very much longer with this emergency situation.
Much as I commend the amendments the minister has brought forward with respect to the National Housing Act. I do not think he
National Housing Act

has gone nearly far enough. The bright boys of the department are still thinking in terms of building priorities and we are away past that stage. I am suggesting to the minister therefore, as strongly as I can, that he give some attention to part II of the act, to see that low-cost public housing is started in this country, so that we may get back substantially to the recommendations of the Curtis report of 1943, which made provision for housing which, I think, is most necessary and imperative at this time.

speechtext:
This house has threshed a terrific lot of old straw, it seems to me, in connection with matters relating to housing, and I think a great deal of credit is due to hon. members on all sides of the house for taking the responsibilities of their office sufficiently seriously that, after these arguments have been presented in brilliant form in many cases and so many times in this house since I have been a member here, they are not content to let the government rest until a better approach than our present feeble effort in housing is put forth by the one man in this country who is able to do the job if he would get on with it; I refer to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe).
The National Housing Act has been analysed in so many ways in this house that I simply want to indicate once more that under part I of the act the loans last year were 6,927. In housing emergency that is really a terrific national effort, is it not? Under part II of the act, which provides for rental housing loans, we were able to lay out money for 4,836 houses.
Part III of the act, which provides for federal funds for farm housing, is not even yet proclaimed by the government of Canada. Part IV of the act deals with the home improvement feature. Actually fifty-three units in Canada were repaired under the terms of that part. There was a certain amount of research carried on under part V, largely in the statistical field and none in the scientific field. There was spent $160,000 under this section, of which $85,000 was for economic research; $3,000 for architectural investigation; $70,000 for community planning; $3,000 for educational work and nil under technical research. All these figures come from the government's own factual summary "Housing in Canada", presented in January, 1947.
With respect to the whole matter of housing, I think the minister acts as though he intends that the government will just get out of the housing business entirely and leave it to free enterprise, because, while we have certain statutes on the books, the physical pro-

cess of house building is not being accomplished. The amount of money which we have spent and the amount we are providing for next year indicates that the government is gradually getting out of the picture. I want to present two tables to the house. One is with respect to the estimates of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply for the coming year, dealing with housing.
571. To provide for payments of amounts ow'ing under guarantees pursuant to item 60 of schedule A to the Appropriation Act, No. 6, 1946 (and pursuant to corresponding items in previous appropriation acts) to approved lending institutions in respect of loans made for the purpose of financing the conversion of existing houses into multiple family houses, such payments to be made out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, $1.
There is a nominal item of $1, owing to the fact, I presume, that the government has not anticipated any losses. Under home conversion plan, item 572, the government proposes this year to reduce the estimate of last year by $250,000, making an expenditure of $250,000 for the ensuring year. Under emergency shelter, administration, the estimate is $2,000,000, a reduction of $297,000 from last year. On Wartime Housing Limited in the ensuing year they propose to spend $27,500,000 by contrast with an estimate of $42,000,000 last year, a drop of $14,500,000. That is the financial picture under the plan of the department of reconstruction. They make provision for a potential expenditure of some $30,000,000 at a time when we have an admittedly serious crisis in housing.

That is roughly double what the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is proposing to ask this house for with respect to the ensuing year. It is interesting, of course, to note the way in which that budget is broken up with respect to provision for rental housing facilities for large families, for workmen's families and for rural families. The Swedish budget provides for the expenditure of money in manners that the Canadian government is not yet prepared to accept as an obligation of the Dominion of Canada.
I think we should examine as well the particular Bill No. 176 which the minister has before the house at the present time. I am willing to concede that there are one or two good features in the bill. But as has been said by everyone who has spoken this afternoon, there is a piecemeal goodness about it. There is, for example, the increased ratio of lending value to the cost of construction. However, that is not an unmixed blessing, because with the terrific rise in building costs -which the government has permitted by its decontrol policy-it simply means that the individual who is lucky enough to be able to make a down payment on a house is putting down approximately the same amount now, with rising costs, which he might have put down, a year or two ago under lower costs; and at the same time, because of the high cost, he has increased his liability for years to come. Therefore I say that, while the fact is that a man is able to buy a house with a smaller percentage of equity under this new proposal, it will not in fact give him as great an equity in his house as could have been arranged by assuring that building costs remained down. The amortization period is extended from twenty years or, under certain conditions, twenty-five years, as it was before,
to thirty years. That is a feature which should be commended. In my opinion, a third good feature is the provision for direct loans by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation where lending institutions may, for certain reasons, not want to lend money to a prospective home owner.
I consider it my duty to draw the attention of the minister to some of the bad features in this bill. The improvement of land is one of the main things provided for. Under that provision housing groups or mortgage companies or land companies may develop housing areas in suburban districts and the cost is guaranteed to those companies by the people of Canada. Such companies are permitted to make two per cent on their investment. In my opinion that, in effect, is a future subsidy to those companies and to the families to which they hope the properties will be sold. I can guarantee to the minister that, with present costs, those houses will not be houses that can be purchased by low-income families. I think he will have to agree with that statement. In my opinion that is a bad form of subsidy. I believe in the subsidy principle with respect to housing, but it should be applicable at the low-income and wage levels.
There is another feature which the minister and his officials have overlooked entirely and I should like to draw his attention to it at this time, because we propose to submit an amendment in committee to remedy the defect. As I see it, there is a danger that the maintenance costs for the suburban developments provided by this bill are likely to be loaded on the municipalities. The experience in connection with former housing developments in suburban areas has been referred to by previous speakers this afternoon. By this legislation, the development companies are protected from going bankrupt; we as the people of Canada are preventing those companies from going bankrupt, but many of the facilities which will be needed to make these areas habitable, such as streets, roads, water facilities, schools, utilities of various kinds, will have to be provided by the municipality. As far as I can see, there is no provision in the act to permit the municipality or the provincial planning board to take any part in the planning of this work.
I have here figures from the official United States records indicating that in 1935, when there was not a great deal of suburban development, the city of Boston found that its revenues per resident from the suburban area was $47 a year, whereas the expenditures
National Housing Act

on facilities for those suburbanites was $63 per resident. If this bill is permitted to be carried through and this work is carried on without consultation with the provincial or municipal government concerned we can envisage, not the bankruptcy of the speculators in suburban development, because they are protected by the government, but the bankruptcy of the municipality itself. Pressure will be exerted upon the municipality to extend public facilities, to build roads and all the rest of it, while the people who will exert this pressure upon the municipality will be protected against personal loss by the federal government under the terms of Bill No. 176.
Ancillary to this is the fact that there is no provision for the expression of opinion by local planning bodies with respect to the type of community to be built as a result of the enterprise which is being sponsored under this bill by the minister of reconstruction. As far as I can see, there is no provision for participation in any form by planning bodies which have been set up by municipalities or which are envisaged under the terms of different provincial statutes.
The final criticism-and this is an old one from the point of view of hon. members in this corner-is that there is no provision for participation in this fund by provincial or municipal housing authorities that have been set up or that may be set up in the future. As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) said in the brilliant speech he made a few minutes ago, we are going to vote for this measure, but we are disappointed that it goes only such a short way to meet the problem facing us. We feel certain that this bill will not take us many further steps along the road to providing houses for the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or two with regard to this subject. I do not think it is necessary for me to remind the house or the people of Canada of the urgent need there is for more housing. We are all aware of that fact, and the attention of the government has been directed to it on more than one occasion, not only at this session by hon. members who have spoken already but in previous sessions.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) referred to the fact that the government should continue the same type of housing programme in peace time as they used during the war. I hope I am not misquoting the hon. member, but that was what I understood him to say. I do not agree with that. I think the
houses which the government built under the national housing scheme are much superior to those built under any other housing programme the government has instituted.

* Mr. JOHNSTON: I think you will find that in his speech. Possibly what he had in-mind was that the government should carry on that type of mass production which it carried on during war time. That was my understanding of it, anyway. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), who spoke a few minutes ago, suggested a continuation of the government's plan for mass production under government ownership. I should like to point out to the hon. members for Mackenzie and Cariboo that I have watched very carefully the different types of houses that have been built. It is my opinion that, except in one or two particular instances, the majority of the houses built under Wartime Housing or the veterans housing scheme do not begin to compare with the houses built under the national housing scheme. I have made the statement before and I do not hesitate to repeat it, that I believe it is better business; I believe it will result in more satisfaction to the men who receive these houses if we build one house properly rather than build two houses which inevitably will fall down in a few years. It is my view that in respect of a large number of the houses now being built by the government, such as those under Wartime Housing or under the Veterans' Land Act, the municipalities, both rural and urban, will be faced with a bad situation in years to come. I hesitate to refer to them as slum areas, lest some may take the wrong impression from my words. But I do not think one could use any other expression if he wished to convey a proper picture, and particularly when one thinks of the houses which were built in Hull, just across the river, during war time.
For the moment I should like to speak about the financing of these houses, and in that connection I would commend the hon. member for Cariboo upon the suggestion he made. That very thing has been in my mind. I do not think it is possible for the government to finance a large housing programme under the present financial arrangements set out in the contracts. I would assume that in respect of national housing the government is using exactly the same type of contract agreement as it is using in other types of housing. If I am wrong in that, the minister will correct me. I say that, however, because I believe it is a standard form of contract.
[Mr. Probe. 1

National Housing Act
Lnder it, as I pointed out before, those who are purchasing or building these houses are required to pay i>, per cent compounded half yearly. As the hon. member for Cariboo pointed out, on the incomes these people are receiving, including both civilians and veterans, it is absolutely impossible for them to pay those large sums of money at that high rate of interest over the period of time allotted in the contract, or the extended period allotted in the bill before us. I suggest that the minister should give careful consideration to devising some scheme whereby the national credit of the country could be used to give these people decent homes, and at an interest rate sufficient only to cover service charges.
I should like to refer to another aspect of the matter, and in this connection I again refer to the contract. The reference I am about to make would apply to veterans who are affected by different types of government housing programmes, as well as to those who are building houses under the National Housing Act programme. I believe every consideration should be given to the man who is purchasing one of these houses. It is a lifetime investment for him, and a tremendous amount of money that he is required to invest.
I suggest that every time a man makes a payment it should be recognized that to that extent he has a definite equity in the home. I do not believe the contract should be worded as it is today, so that the lending agency is in a position whereby, should the builder, civilian or veteran be unable to pay his required instalment, it can evict the individual affected. I know it might be said that the mortgage companies or lending companies would not do that. But I know of actual cases where mortgage and lending companies have done that very thing, although not under this legislation.
There should be some protection for individuals who are building these homes. When a man has made payments amounting to six or seven thousand dollars and then suffers some misfortune and finds that he must miss two or three payments, it seems most unfair that a lending company should be in a position to dispossess him of his entire property, and the equity therein.

The property should be resold, not just to anyone the company might select, or at any price it might set, but to the highest bidder and at a reasonable price. Then, after the actual expenses of the sale wore deducted from the proceeds, the remainder should be returned to the man who originally entered into the contract with the company.
This would be unjust neither to the company nor to the man who bought the house. It would not deal unfairly with the government. If any of the three is financially able to take the loss, surely it would be either the company or the government, but certainly not the individual.
I have only a word more to say in the matter, and I have no desire to detain the house beyond six o'clock, particularly if it is the wish to have this measure passed today.
I would however suggest to the minister that he review the contract. I draw it to his attention particularly as it applies to veterans under Wartime Housing, but not so much in respect of National Housing, which concerns a different class of people. I suggest that the minister might give this matter his consideration with a view to making some change in the contract so as to give a purchaser of one of these homes a fair and equitable share in the property he is acquiring.

Before the debate is closed, I wish to discuss briefly a matter which affects my own constituency, which is, I believe, of general interest to the country. Some time ago the minister announced in the house that the corporation known as Housing Enterprises had for the most part decided to drop its building project for this year. I hold in my hand a clipping from a newspaper that appeared the day after the minister's announcement. This article gives certain information on that. Here are some of the reasons that were given after the minister made his announcement. I am not sure which paper this is, but I think it is a reliable one. It says:
Because of the continued high cost of material and labour and subsequent failure to provide low rentals, Housing Enterprises Limited, operated by the life insurance companies under the National Housing Act, has decided to drop its 1947 building programme, Reconstruction Minister C. I). Howe told the house this afternoon.
Then a little further on, the following appears:
The situation was brought to a head when a firm bid was received for 400 units in Hamilton and which bid would result in rentals of from $55 to $75 for three, four and five-room units respectively.
Further on, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), the minister said:
The rents being charged in the Toronto area were so high that they were not in the class of low-rental housing. They ran between $45 and $55 a month.
I put that on the record because it has a bearing on what I want to say about Housing Enterprises. I believe that the experi-
National Housing Act

ment which was perhaps entered into in good faith by the government with this corporation, which is a holding company for the life insurance companies of Canada, has not produced good results. I also wish to say that it is strange that the results produced were as meagre as they were when one realizes what concessions this company received from the government.
I have had a little personal experience with this corporation because it so happened that one of the concessions it received was the privilege of buying one of the airports at Dauphin, No. 10, and the terms of the sale, as well as the way in which it came about, created a great deal of interest and not a little indignation in the town of Dauphin and in the district. It appeared that before any of the locally interested bodies had received any notification or any warning that this airport was to be sold to Housing Enterprises, men were already on the job ready to tear down the buildings. However I am not going to labour that part of it because there may have been some misunderstanding there. But the part that is important is that this corporation has received from Central Housing Mortgage Corporation a concession which should have made it possible to construct many more houses than have been built and at a lower price, and houses which could have been let at lower rentals.
For example, in the case of the airport at Dauphin to which I have referred this company was given the privilege of buying thirty-two of the forty buildings that were sold. According to a return which I received, the original cost of these buildings was 8799,450. Housing Enterprises paid for all these buildings a total of $64,120, or eight per cent of the original cost. In addition to this, the original cost of putting up these buildings-some of them were constructed in 1940 and some in 1941-was much lower than it would be^ at the present time because costs of materials were considerably lower. As a matter of fact, I happen to know that the contractors who took contracts to put up buildings in this airport went out to the farmers and, in some cases, under false pretences bought lumber from the farmers at as low as 820. After the company had received a concession of that kind, I was surprised to find, in the course of a conversation with one of its officials, that they had not contracted to build one building in Manitoba. They also bought an airport in the town of Virden. Another return I have here informs us that in the town of Virden they bought buildings that originally cost
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
$463,730 at a price which worked out to a little 'less than six per cent of the original cost.
We find also that, while Housing Enterprises had not contracted to build any houses in Manitoba, they were given the privilege of coming in and buying up these airports and shipping the material out of Manitoba, some of it going as far west as Regina, Edmonton and Vancouver, and some of it going to Toronto. On top of that, we find that Housing Enterprises had the right to sell to the public on the spot any material which they did not require for their own purposes. Apparently the prices at which they sold were based practically on the prices of new material. We found that, in. connection with No. 10 airport in Dauphin, people who came to buy space heaters, which the company bought at the rate of eight per cent of the original cost, which works out at from $31 to $33, were charged, first, $100 and then $150; then, when the demand was great the price went up to $200, and in the end these space heaters were selling for $225 each.
It was the same story with washbasins, sinks, toilets, linoleum and so on. For example, washbasins which were incomplete because the trap was missing were $13 each; sinks, $12.50; toilets, $16; linoleum, $1.75 a yard, and so on down the 'line. Shiplap, for instance sold at $45 per thousand and dimension lumber, the bigger sizes, up to $50 per thousand. AVhen the citizens of Dauphin and district discovered that this company was tearing down the buildings at this airport and shipping materials out of Manitoba, at the same time making a huge profit on scrap material sold on the spot, they decided to make a protest.
I am not going to repeat the whole story here because the minister is familiar with it. Wires were sent in protest-I have copies of all of them-from the citizens of Dauphin and from such organizations as the branch of the legion, the board of trade of the town of Dauphin, the rural municipality, and so on, protesting that before the local authorities had had any opportunity to make provision for buying these buildings and supplying the material for local use, particularly to veterans who had begun building houses and had not the material with which to finish them, this company walked in and got a number one priority because they happened to be classified as a government agency under the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, having the privilege of making a huge profit on scrap material.
As a result of these protests, the officials in Winnipeg did make an arrangement with Housing Enterprises to release a certain

National Housing Act
amount of that material for the local use of veterans, and there again I have a protest to make, because we were given to understand that the prices to be charged by Housing Enterprises would be reasonable. No figures were stated at the time, but an estimate was given for lumber of from $25 to $30 a thousand. When the material was made available we found that the veterans were charged $45 or $50 for the same material. The same applied all down the line.
The objection I have is this. The government is going to spend millions. It is well known that Housing Enterprises have the privilege of borrowing up to $90 million on the dominion treasury, putting up $10 million of their own capital, being guaranteed the investment back again and a profit of at least two per cent. In other words, they do not take any risk whatever bu* are using the money of the policyholders of the life insurance company, investing it, and being guaranteed a profit. They are getting a return on their investment and are also given the privilege of buying up airports which could be made far more useful in local communities or in the provinces where they are. But in spite of all these concessions, we find that today the whole project has turned out to be one big fizzle.
I feel that if the government is going to be justified in spending $90 million or any amount of that size, the money would be far better spent if the government would do as was suggested this afternoon to my Tight-get in touch with the provincial authorities and the municipal authorities and offer them the same concessions as, or even better concessions than they offered Housing Enterprises. I believe that, because these authorities have some responsibility to the public, they would see to it that houses were built and rented at cost.
The more we study the agreement between Housing Enterprises Limited and Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation, the more we realize that the whole scheme does not look genuine. The whole scheme is worked out in such a way that Housing Enterprises cannot lose; and when we realize that, after having received a loan, after having been guaranteed a profit, the houses which they build belong to Housing Enterprises, and after payments have been made for a period of fifty years they still own the houses, we can understand the situation. It is true that some houses after fifty years will not be worth much, but some will be worth a considerable amount of money, and there is no reason why a private company should be given such a plum at a time when houses are badly needed.
If the government had spent the same amount of money, or had risked the same amount of money and given the same concessions to the municipal and provincial authorities, we -would have had houses at a lower rental price and it would have been more satisfactory all round.
I am particularly worried about the fact that in such communities as Dauphin and other towns of that size, where the local authorities were interested in doing something about houses, they found almost overnight that the airports -which should have been made available to them were suddenly sold to someone else. Somebody comes along and takes all the material and ships it out of the province, and nothing is left for the local people.
The minister is aware that in the town of Dauphin there was organized a veterans' company, consisting of returned men, who were willing to buy either of the two airports there, tear it down, and make the material available to the local people for building purposes. That company was not even consulted, or let in on the deal at all. The company knew nothing at all about the matter until Housing Enterprises walked in and took the airport over.
What was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), although it sounds like a new line of policy from that side of the house-

If you want to get political I will start in the right place. During the last two years, we have been hearing nothing but private enterprise from members of the Progressive Conservative party in regard to housing, but today they admit that it takes the government and the provincial and municipal authorities cooperating to get houses built, I have not heard the words "private enterprise" mentioned once in the whole debate.
I believe that if the line of action I have outlined were taken the government could retrieve something out of this muddle that has resulted from the breaking down on the project of Housing Enterprises. The government realizes today, as hon. members do, that the reason why low-rental housing will never result from the operations of private firms building houses is that these firms are not in the business of building houses for the use of the people but for making a profit.
I am not going to argue now the question whether making a profit is wrong, but the objective is more houses and lower rental houses, and it is up to the government to invest every dollar possible in this project on
National Housing Act

a non-profit basis. The experiment with Housing Enterprises has been perhaps a lesson. It has been a costly one.
I find from another return that during the past year this firm was advanced loans totalling over $16 million, and the result of all that has been that only a limited number of houses-I have not the figures here-were built, and houses which originally were planned to be rented at $35 a month have now to be rented at $55 or $65 a month.
I also want to register a protest on behalf of Dauphin and other communities in Manitoba where airports were bought and wrecked without the local people having an opportunity of receiving the materials they required.
I am not going to take more of the time of the house, because some of the other material I have can be used perhaps on the various sections of the bill. I want to say emphatically that the results of the experiment in the last two years have proven that if we are to have low-rental housing it will have to be done through public enterprise, through local authorities cooperating with the dominion government, with the objective of providing houses and not making profits.

I presume, when the minister speaks, he will close the debate. If I might have an opportunity to say or word or two I promise you, Mr. Speaker, that I will not read my speech, which has not been my habit for two or three decades. I should like to make one or two general observations with regard to this question which seems to be gripping the imagination of the Canadian people. To my mind, broad enough consideration has not been given with regard to the real wants with regard to housing. It seems to me that our people-perhaps on account of the tragic war we have come through-having been brought to the large centres to ply their handicrafts in the art of making war material, are not desirous of going back to the place whence they came. If your department, sir, would give some thought to the reason for this shortage they would perhaps find that in yesteryear many of those now seeking housing accommodation in the large centres of population could find abundance of housing accommodation in the counties of Ontario, for example, or in the counties of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick. I cannot speak so well for what provision there is in western Canada to house our people. But no one in this chamber can gainsay the fact that there are scores of houses vacant in the back country, one might call it. or in the country portion of Ontario and the other provinces.

They are nice houses, but are a little old, and need a little repair and attention. They are surrounded by an abundance of the best farming country anywhere in the civilized world, off which people could get a good living.
In spite of all the discussions which have taken place in this chamber, I have yet to hear hon. members advocating that these houses vacant throughout the length and breadth of our land should be utilized. No encouragement. is being given to a movement to get our people back to those vacant properties. Why not, sir, within your department, have every county council within our province make an index of the number of vacant houses and vacant farms within their county and file that with the responsible party? Then instead of, as I sometimes feel disposed to say, wasting propaganda on our people in telling them what they should and should not do, let us have a little propaganda directed toward our people who are seeking housing, asking them to go back to mother nature, to go back to some of these good homes and lands which are lying vacant at the present time.
A quarter of a century ago, it was my high privilege to live on lot 30, concession D, Scarboro-if you will pardon a personal reference-on which there was a little four-roomed house where my family lived on some twenty-five acres of land. From there I took a seat in this honourable house. Looking back on those days, I say to the young men and the young women-part and parcel of the last war-who did so much for us, that after the first war I found myself in that position. Looking back, I say they were the happiest days of my short term of existence in this world. I enjoyed them immensely. Twenty-five acres and a four or five-roomed house built partly by my own hands helped me to understand how easy it was to make a living in this fair land of Canada.
I am saying this now, not for the edification of this honourable chamber but so that those many thousands who are looking for some place in which to live and eke out an existence in the urban sections of our community, may have their sights changed a little, may go back to the land and find how easy it is there, at their age, to make a living. Most of those about whom we are thinking tonight are perhaps between twenty-five and forty or forty-five. I want them to see how easy it would be for them to make a living and to find housing accommodation at very little expense. If they must follow a trade; if they must find their vocation in a city or a town, has there not been a tremendous development in the

National Housing Act
matter of transportation in the last quarter of a century? Is it not easy to get to town if the town is ten, fifteen or twenty miles away? If they cannot afford their own T-model Ford, as it were, they can still find, close to many of the large centres of population, all sorts of transportation services to take them to their jobs within the community.
With the least little bit of ambition, in these days when people are demanding an eight-hour day and perhaps working only about seven hours and getting eight hours' pay, much might be done. There are today sixteen more hours left in the day. Thirty years ago, while punching a time-clock at seven o'clock in the morning and again at six o'clock at night, six days in the week, more money was made by one individual in this chamber between the hours of six o'clock at night and seven o'clock the next morning on twenty-five acres of land than was made at the job he had at the factory where he punched a time-clock. Nowadays a job which pays good wages and this other little bit of endeavour after having put in eight hours a day-we need only eight hours' sleep-could give a bountiful living to those of our Canadian citizens who today find themselves looking for a house in which to live and looking, if they only knew it, for some little chore to help occupy those extra eight hours; not the eight hours that he works for someone else, not the eight hours which he requires for his sleep, but those eight hours of working recreation. My recommendation, sir, is that the eight hours of recreation should be spent in some of these thousands of vacant lands in the rural parts of Ontario and the other provinces, which are not too far away from where the individual can find a job. If that is done I think, in the final analysis, we shall have within Canada a stronger and better race of people.
I have trespassed on your time for no other reason than to bring to the attention of the Canadian people the fact that we are not doing right by our country when we allow thousands of farm homes to remain idle when thousands of our people are trekking to the industrial centres and are unable to find roofs to put over their heads. They are more and more becoming the type of people whom some of us in this chamber encourage to lean on the government instead of on themselves, instead of applying themselves in the grandest land that civilization has ever known, our country, Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not any thought of entering into this discussion on housing, although I
did spend some time this afternoon listening to the hardship stories of some of the hon. members of the opposition until I found myself on the verge of tears. I have been rather quiet on this subject; as a matter of fact, I have been rather quiet on all subjects during this session. Perhaps one reason is that I formed the habit of talking to my people every two weeks for fifteen minutes through the local broadcasting station. That may have acted as a safety valve and I have not found it necessary to take up much of the time of the house.
When I came back tonight and found that the discussion on housing was still continuing I started to tell a story about housing to one of my friends outside. This incident came to my attention not long ago and I had used it in one of my broadcasts. I went up to my office to get a copy of that broadcast and I found that it was even more like a Ripley story than I had remembered. Then I came into the chamber and heard the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) talking my language and that encouraged me to go on to tell my story of housing.
This incident happened this spring. I was driving along with a fellow and he told me that he had built a bungalow in Pembroke, twenty-five feet by twenty-five, complete with basement, full wiring, painting, decorating and all that. He had built this home while working a ten-hour, rather than an eight-hour day. I do not know whether his wife helped him with digging the cellar, but in any event it was dug by hand. He and his wife ran the cement for the cellar and they built their home without any additional help. This was all done while he was working at a well paid job ten hours a day. He did what is advocated by the hon. member for Danforth. He is a young, healthy, strong chap who came from the farm and knows how to work. He happened to have in reserve a bush lot from which he cut his own lumber.
When he finished his story I asked him if he had any idea how much cash he had invested in the bungalow. Believe it or not, this is what he told me. He said he could not be sure because they had not kept accurate accounts, but their best guess was $600. He said it was $600, not $6,000. I just wanted to give hon. members the details of this instance where a bungalow was built in Renfrew county, in the town of Pembroke.
I can give the house another incident. My wife and I live in a little cottage in Westboro. A little more than a year ago an air force man bought the lot alongside where we live. He was not a carpenter, but he was young
National Housing Act

and strong and willing to work. Occasionally he would get in one of his pals who knew more about carpentry work than he did. He has not a basement, but they got in their foundation and a roof over part of the building. His wife and son moved in and they lived there all summer. They accomplished enough to permit the family to live there during the winter. They are still working away at their home, but it is almost complete and it will be a beautiful place in which to live. I do not know how much cash it has cost him, but he has something to show for the work he put forth on holidays and nights, sometimes well up to midnight. As the hon. member for Danforth has said, if you are young it does not hurt you to work until midnight even at such strenuous work. This offers much in the way of a solution for our housing problem, this sort of effort on the part of individuals.
A few blocks over, another air force man did the same thing. He built himself a home and he moved there with his wife and child. Then he was transferred to Toronto and he sold his home for $3,500. I do not know how much of that was profit, but I want to endorse what the hon. member for Danforth has said. I wanted to point these incidents out as being, in part, a solution for the housing problem in this Canada of ours.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, I think I can compress what I have to say on this matter into the space of four or five minutes.
As far as the bill itself is concerned, there is nothing of any great importance in it. It contains routine amendments to the act and takes some of the strictness out of certain provisions. However, the bill has provoked a debate on some of the wider aspects of the housing problem. I am not going to review everything that has been said about housing conditions in Canada during the course of this debate, because all of it sadly is true. I think conditions are worse now than they have been at any time.
The fault does not lie in the terms of the National Housing Act; it lies with the administration. I think the time has come when we should have from the minister a comprehensive report on the housing situation in Canada. The house will remember that the minister made a comprehensive report on July 22, 1946, the first report of its kind for some months. All we have had this session is mere fragmentary reports.
The latest development is that Housing Enterprises Limited has come to a standstill. 
I should like to read three or four sentences of what I said on this subject on March 22, 1946, as follows:
Housing Enterprises Limited has announced that its objective in 1946 is the construction of
6.000	housing units in various Canadian centres. That is rental housing. That is a drop in the bucket. Let us not delude ourselves that this will be low-rent housing. It cannot be. The cost of construction today is such that Housing Enterprises Limited cannot build low-rent housing as that term is properly understood. They will probably be medium-rental houses.
Now, in May, 1947, the minister has announced that, because Housing Enterprises Limited cannot build low-rental housing, it has brought its operations to a standstill.
Then, bearing on the matter of the need for a report, may I remind the house of what the minister had to say on this subject when he spoke on July 22, 1946, as reported at page 3672 of Hansard:
As at March, 1946, our minimum immediate housing needs were estimated at 150,000 housing units. This figure is equal to the number of houses which under normal conditions would have been built during the war years to keep up with the increase in the number of families.
And farther on, he had this to say:
I believe that these figures and estimates, although approximate, are valid and that we can anticipate by spring 1947, an immediate housing deficit of some 180,000 units, or a worsening of the situation by some 20 per cent.
I think the house is entitled at this stage to know what is the present estimated housing shortage, according to the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or of the department presided over by the minister. I would remind the house that the estimate of an immediate emergency housing shortage of
180.000	units as at March 31, 1947, was based on the assumption that there would be built in Canada the full 60,000 housing units set forth in the government's housing programme for 1946.
Then, may I say this word in conclusion. Some may complain about the amount of time occupied in discussions in the house with respect to housing conditions in Canada today. The debate today is an example. What has been said may not have been strictly on the bill, because the bill covers a very narrow front in so far as the general problem of housing is concerned. Only four or five amendments are contained in it, and they are not related one to another.
This emphasizes what some of us have been trying to say in the house in the past three sessions, namely, that there should be a committee of the house to deal with this subject. I suggested a standing committee of the house on health, welfare, housing and

National Housing Act
social security, before which reports could be had and where it would be possible to bring officials from the department and officials from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the purpose of securing first-hand information. This would save a good deal of the time of the house.
We do not save time in this chamber by refusing to set up committees of the house to deal with matters requiring intimate and detailed investigation. The housing problem of Canada is far too serious a matter to be allowed to await the time when the government chooses to open up a discussion on housing questions in the house, and to hand out to hon. members, at altogether too rare intervals, prepared statements respecting conditions.
The house has a far greater responsibility with respect to this crucial housing situation than can be discharged by methods of that kind. What we need is a committee before which can be brought first-hand information from officials who can be questioned, so that hon. members may inquire into what they consider to be wrong with the way things are done, and so that they may prod where prodding is necessary to see that proper remedial measures are undertaken. We are not dealing with this problem in the house in what I consider to be a proper and enlightened manner.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having made somewhat lengthy remarks when the resolution preceding the bill was being discussed, it is not my purpose to speak at length on the second reading of the bill. I shall have something to say about the various sections of the bill when we reach committee stage. However we have had a most interesting discussion, and perhaps I should comment on a few matters which were raised in that discussion.
The National Housing Act, which is being amended in the present bill, is the backbone of the financing of house building in Canada at the present time. The bill was amended last year; it is being amended this year, and I have every reason to believe that it will be amended next year, and perhaps at every session of parliament for several years.
The purpose of the amendments is to introduce such changes as may be warranted from year to year to make the National Housing Act an effective method for the financing of house building in this country. The hon.
member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins), in his interesting remarks, suggested that he knew of no building held up for lack of financing. I understood him to say that he knew of no one who had been unable to build a house for lack of money, and that he knew of no builders who had been unable to build houses for lack of money.
That, I think, is an accurate appraisal of the situation. The fact that that is so is due, indirectly, to the National Housing Act. Obviously if borrowing on favourable terms is possible through the National Housing Act, private borrowing must be on a competitive level in order that such private borrowing may continue.
In any event, the result is that cheap and plentiful money has been made available for house building. We have heard the suggestion made tonight that the immediate answer to house building is subsidized state housing. I was surprised to hear that that suggestion came from all parts of the house, including the Progressive Conservative party. I am not closing the door to the possibility that subsidized state housing may be the ultimate solution of the problem; but I do say that if it is to be undertaken there must be quite a different chain of responsibility from the present one. Then, too, there must be a different supply situation, as to both materials and labour, from what exists at the present time.
I would remind hon. members that, under the British North America Act, housing is not a responsibility of the federal government. It comes in the field of property and civil rights, and is primarily the responsibility of the provinces. The federal government has recognized a responsibility for providing housing to take care of the dislocation in population arising through the war. It has been taking an active lead in providing housing for that purpose. But even though it is now taking the lead, it cannot proceed without the active cooperation of the municipalities.
There are great differences in various parts of Canada in the degree of success of housing programmes, and that difference is due wholly to the attitude of the various municipalities. Where a municipality has been cooperative, the number of houses has kept up fully to the requirements of the municipality. If a municipality is uncooperative the best efforts of the government can result only in a partial solution of the situation in that city or municipality. That is inevitable, and one of the handicaps of the department in attempting to provide adequate housing under present circumstances.

National Homing Act

I know of no case in any part of Canada where the government has refused to finance housing under conditions that conform to the requirements of the department. Therefore, if any city, or any municipality, in Canada has not its required housing, the fault is largely in the hands of the municipality. Through its active cooperation, that housing could have been made available.
If subsidized state housing ultimately proves to be the solution-and I have said myself that it may be unfortunate if that must be the solution-then the initiative must be taken by the local authorities, by the provinces and the cities, with the help of the federal government. I think no one will quarrel 'with that viewpoint. That is the only possible way of carrying out housing of that type. That is obviously the proper chain of responsibility.
Mention has been made of slum clearance. There is a great job to be undertaken in slum clearance. But that job must be undertaken through the leadership of the provinces and the- municipalities. Hon. members will appreciate that the federal government cannot go into a municipality and earmark certain blocks for demolition and reconstruction. That is a work for the municipality. I know of only one city which has undertaken any activity in slum clearance, and that is Toronto. As soon as the suggestion was made to the federal government that Toronto wished to undertake a project in slum clearance, part 2 of the National Housing Act was made effective, and assistance under that section was offered immediately to that city. At the present time Toronto, in undertaking that particular project, together with cities in Saskatchewan are the only cities in Canada empowered, under their charters, to enter into and to invest city funds in the housing field. I have seen no inclination on the part of the provinces to urge their cities to accept legislation that would entitle them to enter that field.
Slum clearance is a job that must be undertaken in Canada. It has been suggested that house building would be an effective method of relieving unemployment in time of depression. That is quite true, and it should be used for that purpose. In areas of spotty employment in Canada, the department urges that labour be absorbed in a housing programme. There is no more effective employer of several classes of labour than house building, and slum clearance is a splendid method of providing work where work is needed in low-employment areas. I hope that slum clearance will be used for that purpose. But obviously the time to undertake glum clearance is not at the period of highest employ-

ment in1 the history of this country, at the period when this country was never more prosperous.
Someone mentioned investment in housing in Sweden as compared with Canada. The difference is that housing in Sweden is state housing, and the figures given indicate the full cost of the housing, whereas the figures in Canada indicate only the government's share of housing investment, the bulk of the investment here is being carried by the lending institutions. The full expenditure in Canada on housing is vastly greater than the figures mentioned for Sweden. My department has studied house-building figures in all parts of the world, and we are unable to find any country which has built more houses per unit of population than has Canada during the post-war period.
We set a programme in 1915 for housebuilding in this country-I have mentioned it several times in the house-of 50,000 houses for the first full year after the war. We were able to improve on that. Slightly under
50,000	houses were built in 1945. The target for the second year was 60.000, and in 1946 we built 62,500. The objective is 80,000 for 1947. We have succeeded up to the present time in meeting our objectives. Whether we shall do so this year is in doubt at the moment. Progress of new construction must be much better in the next month or two if we are to meet that objective. The reason is that costs have risen to the point where a new orientation is required to provide houses within the reach of low-income families, and the purpose of this bill is to take steps in that direction. Means must also be found to overcome the shortage of serviced property in or near centres of population. That is another purpose of the bill.
A good deal has been said about Housing Enterprises Limited. I would point out that Housing Enterprises Limited was not a project of the federal government. It was a private corporation which borrowed money under the National Housing Act, just as any other corporation or private individual. It was formed to build low-cost housing. The government has never been happy about that phase of the project. Even in its early stages it seemed doubtful whether it was building a class of housing that this government should endorse as being in the low-rental area. However, the insurance companies had for years been bringing pressure on the government to end government construction. It was claimed that this was a field which should be left to private enterprise. The government has always countered with the answer: If that is your field, why not take some direct part in it? Housing Enteprises was started as a private

venture with the support of the federal government and by invitation of the federal government. The results have been becoming less and less satisfactory. Rentals that looked reasonably favourable in the early stages became higher than could be regarded as favourable in the later stages. When the decision was made by the insurance companies -not by the government-that activity in this field should be ended, the government had no objection.
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) mentioned special concessions to Housing Enterprises Limited. He knows as well as I do that the same price for buildings to be dismantled in the prairie provinces has been made to all priority holders. Practically all the buildings in Saskatchewan were bought by the government of Saskatchewan on the basis that he has mentioned, eight per cent of the original cost. A large number of buildings in Alberta were bought by the provincial government of Alberta at eight per cent of the cost. A few buildings in Manitoba were bought by the government of Manitoba on the same basis. The first priorities go to the dominion, the second to the provinces and the municipalities. For its operations in the housing field Housing Enterprises Limited was considered to hold a first priority. The transaction was perfectly in order and perfectly parallel with the disposal of every building of that type in the prairie provinces. I could continue and go into more detail but I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that further discussion be in committee.

Will the minister tell the committee whether discussions have taken place with the municipalities which would be involved? If we are now proceeding by act of parliament to set up machinery that will allow development to take place adjacent to a city, then naturally the municipal authorities are vitally concerned and will want to know where they stand in the question of providing schools, sewers, parks and driveways. As to this section, I think most of us in the house will be in agreement with the desirability of legislation of this type, having in mind what has been accomplished in the United States by some of the large financial institutions such as insurance companies and others in building housing. While this particular section does not go very far, perhaps it will help to bring about large-scale housing developments which have within them the possibility of good planned development in certain municipal areas. However, the thought that strikes me in reading this section is this. The power to be conferred by this section is hedged around with so many restrictions and conditions that I wonder if many of the financial institutions are likely to take advantage of it. When the legislation preceding this bill was under discussion, our socialist friends to the left made much of the fact that the guarantee of a two per cent return was to be given to these companies, together with the return of their capital investment, and the guarantee was to extend for a five-year period. In relation to the risks and other conditions which are attached, I do not think that can be said to be any great inducement to these lending institutions. The question was asked of the minister as to what conversations had been carried on with the lending institutions to see to what extent they would take advantage of legislation of this kind. I find that the minister said at page 2673 of Hansard of May 1:

institutions. I think the committee would be glad to hear from the minister as to what indication has been given by such institutions as to the extent to which they are prepared to proceed1 with land assembly schemes of the type provided for in this section.

I should like to revert to the matter brought up by the hon. member for Mackenzie, and in this connection I should like to refer to page 4 of the bill. The new section 11B (2) (a) reads:
(a)	the land shall, in the opinion of the corporation, be suitable for a residential housing development.
Throughout the country are many urban and other municipalities which have planning boards of various sorts or master plans for their localities. In many provinces planning acts have been passed which give leads in the matter of planning. However, during the last few years and because of the great housing
National Housing Act

shortage federal agencies have been permitted to cut across the master plans of many municipalities. I think it is only fitting that I should refer at this time to my own city.
Regina is a well planned, pleasant, little city out on the prairie plains. As citizens of that city, we were proud of our accomplishments in the way of general planning. However, various emergency schemes of the federal government came into being and, by dint of necessity, we had to permit the placing of so-called temporary buildings in localities which were not at all suitable for housing. I think the minister and his department would be the last to say that they have furthered the over-all plan for the city.
The temporary nature of these structures does not take away from the fact that they create a situation which does not add to the attractiveness of the urban centre, and I am sure this situation applies in many other places, r should like to have the minister make an addition to the clause I have referred to and I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton:
That section 6, subsection 11B (2) (a) be amended by adding after the words "housing development" the words "and approved as such by the government of the province, the planning body and the municipal council for the area in which the proposed residential housing development is situated."
If that amendment is incorporated it would take care of such matters as were mentioned by the hon. member for Mackenzie in the sense that the municipality would express final approbation of the facilities that are to be used, and the planning authority will sa.y whether or not they fit into the general plan for the area. We would not have the sort of thing that has occurred at Deschenes, near Aylmer, Quebec, where there is an enormous veterans development. Those houses were built in an actual swamp, and in many cases the basements have had to be serviced with pumps installed by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
That sort of thing could have been avoided if the local municipality had been drawn into the picture and consideration given to whatever provincial regulations existed in connection with the matter. If a particular municipality did not want to follow out a plan, that would be their tough luck, but it seems to me that there is a way through cooperation by which the true intent of a housing development can best be arrived at.
