speechtext:
I entertain an even lower opinion of the amendment than that voiced by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who placed his objections on constitutional grounds. As I understood him, he said there is no use in putting in a provision to the effect that the institution concerned
National Housing Act

must obey the provincial law. It must do that anyway. It would be just as foolish and just as futile to enact a provision that a provincial or municipal law should be dispensed with, because it would not have any effect.
I do not believe in parliament putting itself in a position of legislating nonsense or meaningless things. But this amendment is objectionable on other grounds as well. I think in all cases the provinces have enacted legislation which places control over land development in the hands of the municipalities. The province does not attempt to regulate or control the development of land itself.
This amendment proposes to say that, in addition to all the other requirements laid down in the section-and, goodness knows, there are so many of them that I fear it will be little used-parliament should say to every such institution that, having obtained the approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the company must go to the provincial government, which probably has no machinery for dealing with the matter and is not the least bit concerned. Parliament would be saying this, "You have to get the approval of the provincial government, even though the provincial government will not interest itself in the matter." That is why they have conferred jurisdiction on the municipalities. Then, why tie this thing up in reams and reams of red tape-we have enough of it in the section now-and make the situation worse?

I am prepared to admit there may be a certain amount of red tape. On the other hand, we have a duty to perform, and that is to prevent the purchase of land ostensibly for housing development, and then find that nothing is done about it for four or five years. Then, in the event that it looks to the corporation interested that the development may prove to be a white elephant, they will dispose of it just before the end of the five years, to make sure that they have their two per cent profit. Or, if it is successful, they may hold it at the end of fire years, at which time the government's interest in it expires, and they could make a fairly handsome profit out of it. That section 6 be amended by adding, after subsection 11B, subsection 11C:
"(1) Where a municipality has under appropriate provincial legislation power to invest its funds in the purchase and improvement of land to be used for a residential housing development analogous to the power conferred upon a company under subsection (1) of section 11B, and such municipality satisfies the conditions and enters into an agreement similar to that required of a company under subsections (2),
(3)	and (4) of section dlB, the corporation shall guarantee to the municipality a return of investment and interest in the same manner as guaranteed to a company under subsection (3) (c) of section lilB, provided that any lands intended to be included in such housing development which are already owned by such municipality shall be deemed to have been acquired by the municipality as of the date of the agreement with the corporation.

(3)	For the purpose of this section "investment" shall have the same meaning as in subsection (9) of section 11B, saving that the purchase price of any land to be included in the housing development which is already owned by the municipality at the date of tfie agreement shall not exceed the actual cost to the corporation, as may be defined by regulation or the fair market value, as may be determined by the minister, whichever is the lesser."
The intent of this amendment is to put municipal public housing authorities, where such exist or may be set up at a later day, at least on a par with private development companies in the application of this section of the act. As the minister indicated a few moments ago, the city of Toronto has the legal right to take advantage of this act, and urban municipalities in Saskatchewan would also be in a position to take advantage of the act if they were enabled to do so by a section such as this. Many municipalities still own a great deal of land of their own, and they would like to have it developed along lines which they have in mind and which are not related to private development business. For that reason I move this amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon City.

subtopic: INCREASE OF RATIO OF LOAN TO LENDING VALUE UNDER PART I, ETC.
speechtext: This section purports to confer on the corporation power to extend loans in cases that are not covered by sections 4, 8 or 14. These three sections are taken from the first three parts of the act. Section 4 deals with the loan on the house owned by the occupant. Section 8 is taken from part 2 of the act, the rental housing section, and section 14 from part 3, dealing with rural housing. If there are any proper cases not already covered by those sections it seems to me at first blush that we should have appropriate legislation dealing with those cases specifically. It strikes me as anomalous that the government should propose a general provision of this kind saying: We have covered all the cases we can think of by sections 4, 8 and 14, but if we have left any out we are giving a general omnibus power to the corporation to make loans. The terms for a loan are not adequately defined, and the cases are not adequately defined. I question whether a provision of this sort is sound legislation for parliament to enact. I think the minister should have specific cases to lay before us.

Mr. MoKAY: I think we are all pretty well agreed that everything should be done to encourage housing construction, particularly low-rental housing projects. I have been informed that some provincial governments
and cooperative organizations might enter the field if they had some encouragement from the federal government. If it is within the purview of the federal government I believe that it should give the same financial assistance to the provincial authorities which wish to enter the housing field as is given to life insurance companies and other organizations. I feel that this aid should be extended to municipalities, societies and associations such as cooperatives and on the same terms as are. being afforded to others under this act. I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin:
That section 8 be further amended by adding subsection 31B, as follows:
"(1) The minister, with the approval of the governor in council may, on behalf of His Majesty, make a loan to a provincial housing corporation or to a local housing authority for the purpose of assisting in the construction of a low-rental housing project or in the purchase of existing buildings with the land upon which they are situated and their conversion into a low-rental housing project.
(2)	A loan under this authority of this section shall be on the same terms and conditions as those upon which a loan may be granted to a limited dividend housing corporation under section 9 of this act.
(3)	For the purpose of this section, local housing authority shall mean any municipality, society, association, corporation or commission having authority to construct, hold and manage houses built as a low-rental housing project.
(4)	The minister, with the approval of the governor in council, may, on behalf of His Majesty, guarantee to the provincial housing corporation or the local housing authority a net return in any year after completion of the project of three per centum per annum of the cost of_ the project for a period not exceeding the estimated useful life of the project and in any case not exceeding fifty years.
(5)	A loan or guarantee under this section shall, for the purposes of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and section 13 of this act, be deemed to be a loan undier part II of this act.
(6)	The governor in council may by regulation make provision for any matters concerning which he deems regulations are necessary or desirable to carry out the purposes or provisions of this section."

I should like to remind him that in one of his publications, "Housing Progress Abroad," we find on page 1, "Purely on a population basis, Sweden would be about fifteen per cent ahead of Canada." I intimated this afternoon that I thought legislation of this sort should have a preamble that sets out in general terms the housing objectives of this parliament. I mentioned that in the United States and in Australia they have set out what would be considered a reasonable goal. Therefore I should like to move:
That the bill be further amended by inserting the following words before "His Majesty" in the preamble.
"Whereas, the purpose of this act is to provide a programme of housing for the Canadian people that will ensure a separate home in a good neighbourhood for every family who desires to have one.
And whereas, the principle must be accepted that society has reached the stage where a home of good quality and equipment is not only the need but the right of every citizen. Where the family's income does not permit the ownership or rental of such a home, it is the duty of the state to bridge the gap by a rental subsidy.
And whereas, an important objective in realizing this principle is the replacement of slums and other substandard housing, in urban and rural areas, to obviate overcrowding and to progress in an orderly and rapid manner toward a modern standard of housing for the whole Canadian people.	.
And whereas, another objective of great importance is the systematic planning of our cities and neighbourhoods so as to develop _ and redevelop communities which will provide good surroundings for home life and adequate facilities for advancing the industrial and cultural wealth of the nation.	.
And whereas, vital consideration in undertaking the large-scale housing programme envisaged by this act is the undeniable fact that a stable level of construction throughout the years immediately ahead is one of the most necessary factors in ensuring a steady level of employment which, in turn, will provide the buying power essential for prosperity at home and abroad.
Therefore,-"
I am sure it cannot be argued that the accepting of this general objective would, of necessity, commit the government to any definite expenditures until they saw fit to bring in a particular proposal. It is merely an outline of what I think should meet with the
whole-hearted support of the minister. The cost over the next ten years would be much less than the expenditures the minister undertook in connection with carrying out his responsibility while Canada was at war.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Railway Act to make provision, inter alia, for an increase in the salaries of the commissioners and for an annual grant of two hundred thousand dollars for a period of ten years towards the maintenance of the railway grade crossing fund.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Will the minister make a statement.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
The bill which is based on this resolution will seek to increase the salaries of the members of the board of transport commissioners and at the same time, to pay into the grade crossing fund over a period of ten years the sum of $200,000 a year. I need not read the resolution; it is on the order paper. I think, however, the house will expect me to say something about the reasons which lie behind the decision to increase the salaries of the board of transport commisioners.
The board of transport commissioners was set up in 1903, and I think I can make this general statement, that with but one exception there has been no increase in the salaries of the commissioners for a period of forty years.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: What is the salary today?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I will come.to that in a moment. I say this, notwithstanding the fact that the duties of the commissioners have increased considerably over the years, as I will indicate in a moment or two.
In 1903. when the board was set up, the salaries of the commissioners were as follows: chief commissioner, $10,000; deputy chief commissioner, $8,000; and the commissioner- because there was only one at that time- $8,000. In 1908, when the number of the board was increased from three to six, the salaries were: chief commissioner, $10,000; assistant chief commissioner, $9,000; deputy chief commissioner, $8,000; and each of the three commissioners, $8,000.
In 1913 the salary of the chief commissioner was increased from $10,000 to $12,500 per annum, and except for that increase having to do with the salary of the chief commissioner in 1913, the salary range stands today as it was forty years ago.
Over the years from 1903 to 1908 the
judicial salaries in the different courts, as well as salaries of officials in other phases of the government service, have been substantially increased to meet changing conditions. The same upward trend over the years has been evidenced, perhaps to an even more marked degree in the salaries paid in various lines of private business and endeavour.
The government in 1930 set up a commission to study the salaries and organization of the civil service throughout Canada. It was known as the Beatty commission, and it brought in a report which recommended substantial increases in the salaries of the board of transport commissioners. However, it was not deemed advisable to follow the recommendations of that commission. Then in 1946 the present government set up the Gordon commission, which made certain recommendations. The recommendations of that commission were that the salary of the chief commissioner be raised to $13,500, that of the assistant chief commissioner to $12,000. and that of each of the commissioners to $10,000. The report made certain other recommendations having to do with superannuation, which I need not go into at the moment. But the government has seen fit to adopt that part of the Gordon report only having to do with salary increases, and has implemented it in the present resolution.

I should have said that the board of transport commissioners, by virtue of the provisions of the Railway Act, is a court of record. The jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners, when it was set

up in 1903, was quite limited. Its powers had to do with the regulation, construction and operation of railways other than government railways within the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. That was general in its terms. But since then the jurisdiction has been extended tremendously. speechtext: To deal now with the grade crossing fund, there has been no payment into the grade crossing fund since the beginning of the war. speechtext:
The resolution provides
for a change of policy. I think I have had as much experience with the board of transport commissioners as any other member of the House of Commons. In 1909 this board was given jurisdiction over telephone and express companies. The bill is to provide for an increase in the salaries of the commissioners. They are now getting the salary of a high court justice and, in addition, they have their travelling expenses, private car and many other things like that. The commission is not carrying out the functions for which it was appointed. When the late Hon. Mr. Justice Mabee was chairman of the old board, it did so and got results.
One section of the Railway Act provides that the board of transport commissioners may, of their own volition, check operations of railroads, express and telephone companies and do other things. Is there any regulation of the railroads in this country today? During the war, a thousand people were killed at level crossings, and it is now proposed to spend $200,000 a year. This is only pin-money. The board is not functioning the way the founders of the board by statute law intended that it should. When Mr. Justice Mabee was chairman he followed the act and summoned the Bell Telephone Company, the express companies and other companies to
Railway Act Amendment

show cause on complaints. The board should carry out the functions for which it was appointed.
It is now proposed to set up a commission to regulate water traffic which is now unregulated. The seamen want such a board. The city of Toronto was forced to spend a $12,000,000 contribution to build a viaduct and harbour and eliminate grade crossings across the whole water front. This $200,000 will largely be spent in one province and it is mere pin-money to help eliminate the level crossing peril. All that they will be able to do is to buy a few bells, wigwags, lights or other means of providing temporary protection. About a year ago the government said to wait until the war was finished and they would show what they were going to do about grade crossings, that they were going to work with the Ontario and other governments. They have provided for large expenditures of money, up to a million dollars, to link in some highways in some of the larger cities. But nothing is being done about grade crossings and these killings will go on just the same.
Another opportunity will be presented when the bill is before us, but I want to say that the railway commission should be doing something to protect the people travelling on our railways. When the late Doctor Manion was our leader, he referred to the government railway as the deadheads railway on account of the huge pass system. The railway commission should look into this whole system of granting passes to see whether there are any abuses. They are not doing it. It is only a minor thing, and I am not objecting to transportation for members of the House of Commons, officials and others, because that is allowed by the Railway Act. But there are many abuses, and I know of some myself from newspaper articles and complaints by letters. There will be other opportunities and I do not want to delay the passing of this resolution. This railway commission should carry out the functions for which it was appointed. We have already had a discussion on this matter of grade separation, during the debate on my bill to amend the criminal code, re deaths at level crossings, and the perils and injury there.

I do not want to oppose the resolution in any way. It is in two parts, one providing for an increase in the salaries of the commissioners and the other for the payment of $200,000 a year over a period of ten years. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister something which happened last Sunday evening which has to do with the railway station at Kingston, and I shall discuss this matter again when the estimates are before the committee. There is a level crossing there, and a definite promise has been made to build a new station at Kingston. What I saw last Sunday evening is a shame and a disgrace. I think the minister will see the same thing at the station at Cornwall.

Railway Act Amendment
Last Sunday evening marked the holiday week-end, and crowds of people were taking the train at 6.30 o'clock that evening. At that time there was a downpour of rain. We talk about railway crossings, but on the proper occasion I intend to draw this matter to the attention of the minister, and, if necessary, to the attention of the Prime Minister. Women and children must hurry to catch these fast trains. The train running between Toronto and Montreal operates in two sections, one of which leaves Ottawa and joins at Brockville. Sometimes the first section will come in first, and sometimes the second.
But at 6.30 p.m. in this downpour of rain, these people had to run for the train. Let me pay a compliment to the train officials who do the best they can under the circumstances. But these trains are undermanned, despite the fact that there are all kinds of men wanting positions today, and among those are returned soldiers. The train officials do not lack in courtesy.
When the train pulled in on Sunday night, what happened? Women and children had to run the length of four or five coaches, past the dining car. Then, when they reach the point where they are to enter the car they find that there may or there may not be a stool to step on. On that occasion I saw a mother running along with a baby in one arm and with luggage in the other. Meantime, if they want to get on the train they must stand in line while forty or fifty people get off, and the others get on. Then, when they get on they go into a full coach, and they must carry their luggage through probably two or three coaches. Surely something should be done about this. Money is being sought for railway crossings, but this is a simple matter.
I think the Canadian National Railways, so far as the Montreal-Toronto service is concerned, needs checking up by someone. I am not referring to the officials, but I say they should have extra help, and the rights of the public should be respected.
There are plenty of nails, and there is lumber available. All that would be necessary would be the erection of what is known as a wooden umbrella to run the length of eight or ten coaches. When the railway estimates are before the committee I intend to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, and, if necessary, to that of the Prime Minister. I have already put it in writing to the president of the railway company, and I am suggesting that something should be done.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
When a grade separation is ordered and the
various proportions of cost are fixed by the board, who carries out the work? Is it the railway concerned?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
As a rule it is the railway concerned; but in certain cases it is by agreement between the parties.
I can think of two or three casgs where it will be done by the railways. When an application is made to the board, the board serves a copy of such application upon the railway and municipality concerned. The railway thereupon sends its engineers to ascertain whether the grade can be separated, and the cost thereof, whether it should be an under-pass or an over-pass, and what the cost will be in each case. Then, when the municipality or other party replies, either for or against the application, the board has all the facts and renders its decision.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: After a hearing.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes. Then the railway builds the separation, generally by giving out the contract after advertising for tenders.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: With respect to automatic signals installed at various crossings, it is my understanding that the materials which go into these signals are not made in Canada. Am I right in that?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Some are and some are not.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Is there a company manufacturing and installing them in Canada?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I cannot say.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I understand there is not. I believe there is no company manufacturing them, and yet when they are brought in there is a duty of forty per cent on the materials coming into Canada. Can the minister tell me whether or not that is correct?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I cannot at the moment, but I shall try to give the information on the bill.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: If they are not manufactured here, why should we have to pay that duty?

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That applies to a lot of other things, too.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I speak
because I am in favour of the principle of the resolution, and particularly the last portion of it, with respect to the $200,000. I think that is a moderate price to pay for the many lives we shall save by grade separation.
Railway Act Amendment

I should like to ask a question with respect to the first part of the resolution. When the time comes, would the minister give us some idea of the amount of work done by the board? I speak with some diffidence because the chairman of the board is married to a relative of mine. I think I should be honest enough to state that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In other words he is an in-law.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Outlaw, did you say?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: No, in-law.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I think there is a great deal in what my desk-mate, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has said, namely, that in earlier years there were periods of construction, quarrels between the railways as to which should go here or there, expropriation proceedings, and movements by people in the various villages and towns to have stations established and agents placed. Then we went through another time when the railways took another view and wanted to close certain lines and certain stations, remove telegraphers, and so on. But my offhand view has been that in the last few years, and certainly up to the time of the undertaking in which they are now engaged, the work of the board has been more limited than it was in earlier days. I hope I am wrong about that, but perhaps the minister would give me a clear statement as to the amount of work going on. I know they do not go west anything like as much as they used to.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: They are certainly working full time now.

subtopic: INCREASED SALARIES TO TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS-RAILWAY GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That is quite true; but this is the only major operation in which they have been engaged for a long time. I can certainly agree that they are busy now, and I agree that proper salaries should be paid to them, or to anyone else, but when we reach the proper stage I hope the minister will be prepared to give us some idea of the amount of work they are doing.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Chevrier thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 255, to amend the Railway Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
